EUobserver https://euobserver.com Independent EU journalism Sat, 14 Nov 2026 08:32:49 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.3 EU leaders hand Ukraine peace talks to France, Germany, UK, Italy, Poland plus Brussels – instead of a single envoy https://euobserver.com/248871/eu-leaders-hand-ukraine-peace-talks-to-france-germany-uk-italy-poland-plus-brussels-instead-of-a-single-envoy/ Fri, 13 Nov 2026 18:54:38 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=248871 As EU leaders began debating who speaks for Europe in Ukraine peace talks, a senior diplomat said sending EU foreign affairs chief Kaja Kallas was “just not possible”.]]> EU leaders agreed at their informal summit in Dublin on Friday that Europe will be represented in Ukraine peace talks by the EU institutions together with France, Germany, the UK, Italy and Poland, rather than a single envoy.

“Today, the leaders agreed that our European team for the negotiations on peace in Ukraine is the European Union institutions and the E5 of the ‘Coalition of the Willing’,” European Council president António Costa told reporters after the meeting on Friday (13 November).

Under the arrangement, the EU will take the lead on Ukraine’s “European future, its reconstruction, and prosperity”, while security guarantees “must be addressed within the framework of the coalition of the willing, in close coordination with Nato”, Costa said.

“Europe must speak with one clear and united voice in all discussions that shape the future of Ukraine and the security of our continent,” he added.

Read more

Trump vows ‘beautiful’ Russia deal, as EU agonises over which envoy to send to Ukraine peace talks

The decision largely formalises the current arrangement, in which France, Germany and the UK sit at the table alongside Italy and Björn Seibert, chief of staff to European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen.

Earlier on Friday, a senior diplomat called that set-up “not ideal”.

It also leaves open whether foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas will take a seat. EU capitals did support sending her to the talks, the diplomat said, adding that it was “just not possible”.

‘Setting traps’

Kallas, for her part, defended her role as she arrived at the summit, and warned that Russia was “setting traps” by trying to divert attention from its aggression with a debate on Europe’s security architecture and the role of Nato.

    ]]>         ‘Very overdue’ – MEPs welcome proxy voting for pregnant members and new mothers https://euobserver.com/248856/very-overdue-meps-welcome-proxy-voting-for-pregnant-members-and-new-mothers/ Fri, 13 Nov 2026 15:39:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=248856 An overwhelming majority in the European Parliament agreed MEPs can delegate their vote to another member in the months before and after childbirth, retaining their say in key files.]]> An overwhelming majority in the European Parliament has agreed that MEPs can delegate their vote to another member in the months before and after childbirth, retaining their say in key files.

    The statute change, passed with 578 votes for, 25 against, and 4 abstentions on Thursday (12 November) will mean that an MEP will be able to vote for one other colleague for three months before, and six months after, childbirth.

    It is “well overdue” that the rules for voting change, Sigrid Friis, a Renew Europe MEP from Denmark told EUobserver. She herself worked up until her due date, provoking some comments about the need for a midwife in the parliament.

    “No member should lose her right to vote because of becoming a mother,” declared the parliament’s president Roberta Metsola in a statement back in April.

    Read more

    MEPs discuss proxy voting for pregnant women and new mothers

    Delegating one’s vote would only apply for the plenary sessions, with both the absent MEP and the one voting for them would be identified in the minutes for transparency’s sake.

    Maria Ohisalo, a Finnish Green MEP, told EUobserver she is “really happy” about the reform.

    “I voted for hours with our baby in the plenary,” she said, recalling her infant was not eligible for child care during the first Strasbourg plenary after giving birth.

    Another MEP who preferred to stay anonymous recalls some colleagues’ annoyance at taking multiple breaks during trilogue negotiations when she was with her newborn.

    The initiative, started by parliament president Roberta Metsola in 2025, still needs an EU Commission opinion and a go-ahead from the council before a final vote in the parliament.

He also urges the use of Russian assets frozen in Belgium, and discussed Baltic expertise in fighting Vladimir Putin.]]> First published in Respekt.

    Estonian prime minister Kristen Michal has laid out how to build up Europe’s defences. He also urges the use of Russian assets frozen in Belgium, and discusses Baltic expertise in fighting Putin. The liberal leader spoke with Ondřej Kundra in early November.

    Has anything brought you satisfaction recently as a politician?

    Kristen Michal: I recently attended the opening of Estonia’s largest timber building in northern Estonia. It may sound amusing this would bring joy to a prime minister, but in my previous role as environment minister, I launched this project in 2023.

    It is a truly beautiful area, both in nature and culture – I recommend visiting. It has a maritime museum in a former seaplane harbour, as well as Estonia’s only submarine. And beside it stands the largest wooden building of its kind: our new natural history museum, under whose roof we want to bring together institutions focused on ecology and climate.

    It is not merely a wooden structure; it is also probably one of most cost-effective buildings, amounting to about €2,100 to €2,200 per square metre.

    One of our state agencies began its construction, and I was genuinely emotional at the opening ceremony – it is rewarding for a politician to see that something they started was actually completed.

    Estonia is one of the foresighted Baltic member states which has warned for years about the Russian threat. EU Commission president Ursula von der Leyen has recognised that Baltic warnings about Russian expansionism unfortunately came true…

    I would probably have been happier if Baltic states had not been right. We spoke about Russia in the past, warning that Putin had imperial dreams of restoring the Soviet Union, that he was not concerned solely with Ukrainian territory, but also with stripping Ukraine of its sovereignty, or that he had further territorial ambitions. It would of course have been preferable if our warnings had not been proven wrong. But they were proven right.

    Even before the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, you warned the West about energy dependence on Russia and about unpreparedness for cyber threats. Now, Europe has learned its lesson. Are you satisfied that EU member states have woken up to reality, or do you think they remain blind to such threats?

    The project is supposed to connect the port of Lobito on Angola’s Atlantic Coast to the mineral-rich Katanga province in the Democratic Republic of Congo and the Copperbelt in Zambia. 

    The European Parliament’s development committee says that the hearing will look into whether the project is effective. 

    EU lawmakers have previously expressed concerns about the governance of Global Gateway, a plan to raise €300bn for infrastructure projects in developing countries that is widely seen as Europe’s response to China’s Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) and the EU’s own urgent need to secure access to critical minerals. 

    The EU Commission says that more than €2bn has already been raised by the EU for the Lobito Corridor project, part of a joint €5bn plan with the United States, as part of close to €150bn in projects across Africa.

    ]]>         The impact of the ICJ’s genocide ruling in Myanmar will go far beyond Asia https://euobserver.com/248744/the-impact-of-the-icjs-genocide-ruling-in-myanmar-will-go-far-beyond-asia/ Fri, 13 Nov 2026 10:21:20 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=248744 On 19 November, the International Court of Justice will deliver its judgement in The Gambia v Myanmar case. The case concerns the Rohingya, but its implications extend well beyond Myanmar. The Court’s interpretation of the Genocide Convention may also matter for the ongoing case brought by South Africa against Israel — and for the credibility of international justice itself.]]> At first sight, a case concerning the Rohingya in Myanmar may seem remote to European readers. But the judgment the International Court of Justice (ICJ) is due to deliver on 19 November addresses questions that go to the heart of international law: when can a state be held responsible for genocide, what evidence is required to establish genocidal intent, and how should the court assess the conduct of state authorities?

    The case was brought by The Gambia, which alleges that Myanmar violated the 1948 Genocide Convention through its treatment of the Rohingya. The court’s answer will matter not only to the victims of the alleged crimes, but also to the interpretation and application of the Convention in other cases.

    One of the most important precedents is the court’s 2007 judgment in Bosnia and Herzegovina v Serbia and Montenegro. Bosnia brought its case in 1993, alleging that Serbia was responsible for genocide committed during the Yugoslav war. In 2007, the court found that genocide had been committed in Srebrenica in July 1995.

    But it did not find that the acts of genocide could be attributed to Serbia. It held that Serbia had nevertheless breached its obligations to prevent genocide and to punish those responsible.

    The distinction is fundamental. The International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY) dealt with the individual criminal responsibility of those who committed or participated in the crimes.

    The ICJ, by contrast, had to determine whether the conduct could be attributed to a state and whether Serbia had breached its obligations under the Genocide Convention.

    Read more

    After students voted out Vučić, can Serbia’s uprising against ‘evil’ change how the state really works?

    The court also set a demanding standard of proof. It held that allegations involving charges of exceptional gravity, such as genocide, must be established by “fully conclusive” evidence, and that it must be “fully convinced” that the allegations have been clearly established.

    Where genocidal intent is not directly established but inferred from a pattern of conduct, the court added that this intent must be the only reasonable inference that can be drawn from the acts in question.

    These requirements attracted criticism. Some considered that the court had effectively approached the question as if it were deciding the criminal guilt of an individual, rather than the international responsibility of a state.

    Others argued that requiring genocidal intent to be the only reasonable inference set an exceptionally high threshold, making it particularly difficult to establish genocide through circumstantial evidence.

    I was an ICTY judge when the ICJ delivered its judgment in 2007. I followed it with particular interest — and some surprise. At the tribunal, we were dealing every day with the individual criminal responsibility of those involved in the crimes committed in Bosnia.

    The evidence concerning Srebrenica and the role of Bosnian Serb political and military leaders was familiar to us. Yet the ICJ was operating within a different legal framework, with a different question to answer.

    Read more

    [Interview] Ex-Bosnia envoy sees no risk of renewed violence, but the fractured country’s EU dream is rotting away

    In its 2015 judgment in Croatia v Serbia, the court largely maintained its approach. It rejected both Croatia’s claim and Serbia’s counterclaim, finding that neither side had established the specific intent required to prove genocide. The demanding standard of proof therefore remains an important feature of the court’s jurisprudence.

    The Gambia v Myanmar proceedings bring these questions back before the court. The judges will have to assess how genocidal intent can be established, including through patterns of conduct and circumstantial evidence, and how the actions of state officials engage the responsibility of the state.

    Myanmar, unsurprisingly, argues for continuity with the court’s established case law. The judgment will show how the court applies that jurisprudence to the evidence before it — and whether it offers further clarification.

    The wider interest in the case is reflected in the participation of eleven states under Article 63 of the court’s Statute: Belgium, Canada, Denmark, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, France, Germany, Ireland, the Maldives, the Netherlands, Slovenia and the United Kingdom. They are not parties to the dispute. They have intervened because they consider that the interpretation of the Genocide Convention is at stake. Under Article 63, the court’s interpretation of the Convention will also be binding on the states that have intervened.

    Belgium’s participation is particularly significant. It is not simply an observer of proceedings taking place far away. By intervening, Belgium has chosen to take a position on the interpretation of a treaty that lies at the centre of the international legal order.

    The judgment will also be closely followed in the case brought by South Africa against Israel. Both proceedings concern the same Genocide Convention, and the ICJ’s reasoning on the interpretation of its provisions, the assessment of evidence and the establishment of genocidal intent may be relevant to the South Africa case.

    The Myanmar judgment will not decide that case, nor should its outcome be prejudged. But the court’s legal reasoning will inevitably attract attention. The two proceedings raise questions that are closely connected, even though their facts and procedural stages are different.

    There is another reason why the composition of the court has attracted attention. Gambia appointed Navi Pillay as its ad hoc judge, while Myanmar appointed the German international law scholar Claus Kreß. Pillay is a distinguished international jurist: she served as President of the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, was a judge at the International Criminal Court (ICC) and later served as UN High Commissioner for Human Rights. In October, she was awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize for her efforts to promote peace and international law.

    Her appointment has nevertheless prompted public comment, particularly because of her previous work and statements concerning Israel. That makes it all the more important to recall the role of an ad hoc judge. Such a judge is not a representative of the state that appointed them. Once appointed, an ad hoc judge has the same duty of independence and impartiality as every other member of the court. I know this responsibility from personal experience, having served myself as an ad hoc judge at the ICJ.

    US sanctions on ICC

    The independence of international judges is not an abstract institutional concern. The ICC has already been subjected to sanctions by the Trump administration, targeting judges and other officials. The ICJ has not faced the same direct measures, but it operates in an international climate in which judicial institutions and those who serve them are increasingly exposed to political pressure.

    The authority of the ICJ ultimately depends on its ability to decide cases independently, according to law and evidence, irrespective of the political consequences.

    The judgment in The Gambia v Myanmar will be important first and foremost for the Rohingya. But it will also help shape the interpretation of the Genocide Convention, influence the debate in other proceedings and test the confidence states place in international adjudication.

    For European countries, this is not a distant legal dispute. Belgium and ten other states have chosen to participate because the interpretation of the Convention matters to them.

    Their commitment to international justice will be tested not only by the positions they take in court, but also by their willingness to defend the independence of the institutions that apply the law — including when the consequences are politically uncomfortable. 

    ]]>         Listen: Is the right to protest under threat in Europe? https://euobserver.com/248738/listen-is-the-right-to-protest-under-threat-in-europe/ Fri, 13 Nov 2026 09:11:01 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=248738 In France, the Senate has just adopted a draft bill that could severely restrict the right to protest. The text still has to go through the National Assembly, but it stands a good chance of becoming law.]]>

    Production: By Europod, in co-production with Sphera Network.

    EUobserver is proud to have an editorial partnership with Europod to co-publish the podcast series “Briefed” hosted by Léa Marchal. The podcast is available on all major platforms.

    Find the full transcript below: 

    In France, the Senate has just adopted a draft bill that could severely restrict the right to protest. The text still has to go through the National Assembly, but it stands a good chance of becoming law.

    Is Europe slowly killing the right to protest?

    Once again, a draft bill has been adopted by the French Senate, with the full support of the far-right Rassemblement National (RN) party.

    The bill was introduced this summer. Its stated aim is to crack down on violent protesters and make them pay for the damage they cause. But it goes much further than that.

    The proposed text targets not only violent protesters responsible for causing damage, but also people who are simply present nearby. They could face fines of up to €10,000, even if they haven’t committed any criminal offence. Simply because they stayed there after the police ordered them to disperse.

    This shifts the burden onto people who may not have committed any offence, while relieving the authorities of the difficulty of identifying the actual perpetrators.

    But opponents argue that this seriously undermines the right to protest. According to Olivier Cahn, a professor of criminal law quoted by the newspaper Le Monde, the wording leaves considerable room for arbitrary interpretation.

    Read more

    Europe’s youth take to the streets as the post‑war promise of a better life breaks down

    In an opinion piece also published in Le Monde, several public figures warn that protesters could find it impossible to prove that they didn’t hear a police order to disperse. In many cases, such warnings simply aren’t heard, either because they aren’t loud enough or because they were never given in the first place.

    The senators have made the bill even tougher by adding a six-month prison sentence for anyone taking part in a demonstration that hasn’t been authorised by the authorities.

    In some cases, the authorities could even seize part of people’s social benefits once they have identified them as offenders. The Senate has gone as far as proposing to evict them from social housing.

    All of this has drawn strong criticism from civil society organisations and left-wing movements. They fear that the bill will discourage people from taking part in peaceful demonstrations because of the risks involved.

    In the opinion piece I mentioned earlier, the authors even draw a parallel with George Orwell’s novel 1984.

    France’s interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, however, believes that the bill has actually been improved by the senators.

    So that’s the situation in France. What about the rest of Europe? Well, let’s just say that a similar trend can be observed almost everywhere.

    Read more

    Europe’s youth asked for hope – but politicians just offer fear and hate

    In 2024, Amnesty International published a major report examining the right to protest in 21 European countries. Its findings pointed to a clear deterioration in the conditions for exercising this right.

    In eight countries, legislation restricting the right to peaceful protest has been introduced in recent years. These are France, Belgium, Germany, Greece, Italy, Luxembourg, Spain and the UK.

    The report’s authors also found that, across all the countries analysed, protesters are frequently labelled as terrorists, criminals, foreign agents, anarchists or extremists.

    People of colour face systematic discrimination in at least seven countries. Climate activists are targeted in almost every country covered by the report.

    LGBTQ+ people, women, children and people with disabilities also face discrimination in several countries.

    All of this, combined with police violence reported in many countries in recent years, is raising concerns among human rights organisations.

    In France, they are now hoping that members of the National Assembly will take a less restrictive approach to dealing with protesters. Let’s see how the debate unfolds in the coming months.

    ]]>         Europe’s self-styled pacifists are helping Putin freeze Ukrainians in their homes https://euobserver.com/248586/europes-self-styled-pacifists-are-helping-putin-freeze-ukrainians-out/ Thu, 12 Nov 2026 19:00:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=248586 As Russia bombs Ukraine’s grid, Hungary, Slovakia, the Czech Republic and Bulgaria want to opt out of the next EU loan - money that actually also helps Ukrainian's civilians build back-up power and heating.]]> As it gets colder and darker, I think of my Ukrainian friends.

    Russian bombing campaigns this year have targeted power and heating facilities, hoping to break morale and leave Ukrainians sitting in the cold and dark come winter. 

    This past weekend alone, strikes on the high-voltage substations around the capital left 80 to 85 percent of Kyiv’s consumers without power. And it could get much worse. 

    Last year, people went without electricity and heating for much of the winter. It was often the elderly, living in poorly insulated older homes, that suffered the most as temperatures dropped to minus 20 degrees.

    The state has so far not succeeded in transitioning from the Soviet-era regulated system towards a more decentralised, more resilient energy system. But that doesn’t mean Ukrainian’s haven’t already started building parts of it themselves.

    I visited the country in May to document how people were preparing for another harrowing winter by building bespoke back-up systems in their gardens, their sheds; on their roofs.  

    Read more

    War is driving Ukraine’s green energy build-out, but lack of money is holding it back

    Across the country, small solar plants and battery storage systems went up to keep hospitals running and to make sure children did not have to sit in the dark in their schools’ bomb shelters for too long. 

    New energy cooperatives have popped up all over Kyiv to pool scarce know-how in a country where the energy system still relies on a handful of giant Soviet-era power plants.

    Áron Orbán on a leash

    For 16 years it had been utterly unthinkable that an official measure could reach all the way into former prime minister Viktor Orbán’s family. Now this has happened. On Monday (9 November), Áron Orbán, the brother of the former prime minister, was taken into custody.     Áron Orbán’s case, which has been taken over by the National Office for Asset Recovery and Asset Protection set up by the new government, is rather convoluted.     In the case, an investigation was launched on suspicion of influence peddling and other criminal offences, but it did not move forward until the elections; afterwards, however, several arrests were made.

    At the start of the week, it looked like prime minister Péter Magyar was heading for a difficult week in office.

Lists published from the archives wrongly identified 164 people, including Fidesz politician Sándor Lezsák, as former agents, when they had actually been victims of surveillance.

    Magyar apologised but argued that the archives are controlled by parliament, not his government. However, since making these records public was a long-promised part of his political agenda, he should take responsibility for the mistake rather than shift the blame.

    On top of that, Magyar also bungled the latest episode of his ongoing political communication soap opera, called Absolute Movie Theater. On Sunday, in his video he showed viewers the lesser‑known parts of the Parliament building, where calendars featuring naked women could be seen on the wall of a basement maintenance workshop.

    Our former colleague Veronika Munk, editor‑in‑chief of 444.hu, directly confronted the issue in an opinion piece, sharply criticising the video, the objectification of women’s bodies and the conspiratorial, primitive machismo.

    The Hungarian prime minister, a prolific Facebook commenter, could not resist weighing in. Commenting under the 444 article, he mocked Munk’s view that crude, breast-focused images are among the most degrading ways women are portrayed in the media. Clearly, he did not agree.

    The former minister did not say much that was new about the case itself, stating that she had had no opportunity to “expose” her former state secretary, Pál Völner, who was up to his neck in the affair.     But Magyar’s superpower is that he can always turn things around. And on Thursday morning (12 November), he did just that.     • They would make the misuse of intimate recordings a standalone criminal offence.
    • They would clearly enshrine the requirement of voluntary consent for sexual acts.
    • They would ensure special treatment for victims of relationship violence in criminal proceedings.
    • They would amend the heartbeat decree. Before terminating a pregnancy, after receiving medical information, the woman concerned could decide for herself whether she wants the signs of the foetus’s vital functions to be shown to her.
    • They would abolish the prescription requirement for the morning‑after pill, so emergency contraception would be available without a prescription.
    • They would launch measures against period poverty, so that those for whom buying basic hygiene products is a financial burden can also obtain them.
    • They would strengthen support for pregnant women.
    • The government will initiate the ratification of the Istanbul Convention. The convention lays down obligations for preventing violence against women and domestic violence, protecting victims and prosecuting perpetrators.

    Is Europe succeeding in combatting violence against women?

    Neither the amendment of the heartbeat decree nor the ratification of the Istanbul Convention featured in Tisza’s election programme.

    Hungary’s new president, András Baka, has shown that he will not automatically approve everything put before him. This week, he refused to sign a government-backed law that could give the state greater influence over investment funds and weaken protections for minority shareholders.

    Baka argued that the law was too broad, could affect existing funds with no state involvement, and offered insufficient protection to smaller investors. He also criticised the fact that it was passed just 26 hours after being introduced, without proper consultation, warning that such unpredictable interventions could undermine investor confidence. He has referred the legislation to the Constitutional Court for review.

    His decision marks a significant departure from the practice of his predecessors, who rarely challenged laws important to the government. For the first time in years, Hungary has a president willing to use his office to question legislation on substantive grounds – a welcome sign for the country’s democracy.

In the total population, 55 percent would currently vote for the governing party, while Fidesz has fallen to 16 percent. This is a low not seen for several decades; they were last this weak in the mid‑1990s.

    With such a vote share, Tisza would win more than 160 seats in parliament if elections were held now. And misfortune is piling up for Fidesz: its more uncertain voters are likely drifting into the camp of non‑voters or to Tisza, while its core electorate and more radical base appear to be eroded by the far‑right Mi Hazánk party.

    So the tables have turned on what Fidesz itself did with the far right for 16 years – it took over its themes, slowly absorbed its voters and turned this kind of political aggression into the mainstream. Now, everything is slowly returning to the “normal order of things”.

    Another survey by Medián has produced data that will make Fidesz scratch its head even more.     Russia faces a strategic crisis and record losses, but thanks to Trump it sees things positively (Ukraine Battlefield update, Day 1,713)

    The problem is that its use completely depends on the goodwill of Elon Musk. But also on the US government. Starshield is a government system, and it’s Washington that actually makes it available to Ukraine.

    This has already led to some awkward situations. A few weeks ago, Ukraine noticed that the speed of its drones had been throttled overnight. The explanation was clear: it was an American move. The issue has since been resolved, but it illustrates a real unease.

    So how did Ukraine end up in this position? At the start of the war, the country’s cable-based internet infrastructure was damaged. On the battlefield, the army now uses SpaceX terminals to receive internet signal, because they’re small and very practical.

    And that is exactly what Europeans don’t offer. Most European satellites are in high orbit. They cover very large areas, but they have two drawbacks in wartime. Because they are further away, the delay in transmission is longer. Second, the equipment needed to receive the signal is much bulkier, so it is not suited to the front line.

    Elon Musk made a very strategic choice: putting tens of thousands of satellites in low orbit.  It’s much cheaper, and much easier to operate. Now could Europeans compete on this market?

    The closest European equivalent, on a smaller scale, is the OneWeb constellation, run by the French company Eutelsat. Eutelsat was originally a European intergovernmental organisation. But it was dismantled and its activity has been taken over by a company.

    The French state is still its largest shareholder, with around a third of the shares. The United Kingdom and an Indian group also hold stakes.

    Through OneWeb, Eutelsat has around 680 satellites, in both low and high orbit. The company says it could replace Starlink in the medium term, meaning sometime in the 2030s.

    It plans to reinforce its fleet with several hundred new satellites. But most of them will actually replace older ones. So it’s not a big increase, compared with Starlink.

    Read more

    Russia’s fake war maps at Abu Dhabi peace talks aren’t fooling anyone (Ukraine Battlefield update, Day 1,721)

    There is also another project designed to secure European connections. It’s called IRIS². This one is a European project, carried out by several companies, including Eutelsat. The EU is its main customer. Unlike OneWeb, it’s not a commercial venture. But both share the same goal: reducing dependence on Starlink.

    The ambition is a constellation of at least 348 satellites by 2030, with deployment starting in 2029. So again, fewer than a thousand. That’s still far from Starlink.

    But here, it’s worth saying that satellites in low orbit are much cheaper to put in place, which also explains the sheer volume SpaceX has been able to launch in recent years.

    With far fewer satellites, but in higher orbit, Europeans can also cover the whole planet. It’s just that the system isn’t as flexible.

    Finally, is money part of the explanation? Yes, of course. The United States spends around six times more on its space programmes, civil and military, than Europeans do.

    There’s also another factor that helps SpaceX deploy thousands of satellites at low cost: it has its own launcher, the Falcon 9.

    Eutelsat, on the other hand, has to buy launches from third parties. So it’s much more expensive, and it doesn’t control the pace at which it can put satellites into orbit.

    Before wrapping up, a quick word about China, another big actor. It’s quite new in the space industry, and it’s not really spending huge amounts of money for the moment. But it’s worth keeping an eye on Beijing on this front too.

    ]]>         The olive branch is a universal symbol of peace – but the West Bank’s autumn olive harvest is open season for Israeli settlers to pillage and kill https://euobserver.com/248241/the-olive-branch-is-a-universal-symbol-of-peace-but-the-west-banks-autumn-olive-harvest-is-open-season-for-israeli-settlers-to-pillage-and-kill/ Wed, 11 Nov 2026 19:00:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=248241 The olive has become much more than a household staple. In Palestine, the annual autumn harvest requires courage, protection by activists and an often deadly struggle. The contrast to Europe's olive tradition has never been so stark.]]> Autumn in Italy is always a special time.

    South of the grey, industrial northern cities, from the rolling hills of Tuscany down to the rocky heel of the Ionian sea, one is never too far from the scent trailing behind the world’s most sought after harvests: the grape, and the olive. 

    I was visiting my family in the fields of Rome, where this year’s crop alleviated concern brought on by last year’s meagre yield. My uncle’s generous green bounty was turned to liquid gold, one that tastes of legacy and belonging.

    On the eastern seaboard of the Mediterranean, it has also come to smell like blood.

    The ancient tradition, and the historic land that binds it to its sturdy tree roots, has been turned into the battleground of Israeli colonisation of the occupied West Bank. Exacerbated since 2023, the olive harvest has become the season synonymous with the most attacks by Israeli defence forces-backed illegal settlers hoping to intimidate Palestinian families out of their homes. 

    Read more

    From West Bank to EU supermarkets: How much longer will Israeli settler imports go on?

    It’s the time where residents, forced indoors in fear of the swelling conflict increasingly taking place beyond just Gaza, dare to set foot out to reap the fruits of the land that provides a living for some 100,000 families across the Palestinian territories.

    Beyond the major source of income many depend upon, depriving Palestine of its olive harvest denies some 5.6 million people with the social fabric that makes up the part of their national identity. 

    According to UN data, the 2025 olive harvest brought 178 settler attacks to the occupied West Bank, in 88 Palestinian towns and villages. Over 6,000 trees and saplings were vandalised.

    ]]>         War of propaganda: Russia calls Ukraine a ‘burden’ and uses Moldova as a ‘testing ground’ to sabotage EU enlargement https://euobserver.com/247967/war-of-propaganda-russia-calls-ukraine-a-burden-and-uses-moldova-as-a-testing-ground-to-sabotage-eu-enlargement/ Wed, 11 Nov 2026 14:32:04 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=247967 From fake celebrity sex scandals to ominous warnings about land seizures and soaring bills, Kremlin-linked campaigns are working to turn ordinary voters against EU accession long before any referendum is held.]]> As the saying goes, the first casualty of war is the truth. But in the case of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, it seems the truth had been under attack for a while. 

    As recently as this summer, claims that Russia had actually made significant battlefield gains were debunked after analysis found that interpretation was based on misuse of a report which actually found Ukraine had made the greater advances.

    It chimes with the continuing battle for control of the narrative over Ukraine, not least when it comes to the prospect of that country, and possibly its neighbour, Moldova, ultimately joining the EU.

    Media organisations in those countries have become acutely aware of what they say is Russian disinformation about EU enlargement, often circulated via the Telegram app and other online platforms such as Facebook.

    They have heard various narratives against EU membership, such as a purported loss of state sovereignty, of the EU wishing to prolong a ‘proxy war’ with Russia through Ukraine, and even of Ukraine being divided up between EU member states.

    As Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine approaches its sixth year, the likelihood of it joining the EU is still being actively debated. Neighbouring Moldova is also driving towards EU membership, even though it is aware that Russia is actively opposed. 

    It means both countries, and others in the region where people have expressed a desire to join the EU, such as Georgia, find themselves the subject of online campaigns which, critics say, are aimed at undermining those efforts.

    Read more

    Moldova seen as ‘best performer’ on EU-accession reforms, despite onslaught of Russian sabotage

    Disinformation is not new

    It is also hard to argue that this is a new phenomenon. Over 10 years ago, the EU set up a task force in order to challenge “Russia’s ongoing disinformation campaigns”. 

    A number of months after the war began in 2022, the OECD think-tank in Paris published a policy paper on ‘Disinformation and Russia’s War of Aggression against Ukraine’, in which it said: “The Russian disinformation narratives are often false, or obscure facts with half-truths and ‘whataboutisms’.” 

    And just last year the delegation of the European Union to Ukraine looked at information manipulation and disinformation that summer targeting Ukraine-EU relations.

    It was a topic of discussion when the deputy prime minister for European integration of Moldova, Cristina Gherasimov, visited Ireland earlier this year. 

    Speaking to The Journal in Dublin last February, Gherasimov said that disinformation “continues constantly”.

    Read more

    How EU hopes to ‘shield’ elections against Moscow’s propaganda

    “This is one of the most powerful tools of Moscow: disinformation, not necessarily about our own country or process in our own country, but a narrative that targets the EU as such. It targets the EU credibility for candidate countries or aspiring countries, for EU membership.

    “Some of the narratives are usually around the future of candidate countries in the EU, saying that we are not ready,” she said.

    This argument, she added, also centred on the idea of the EU as weak and unable to stand up for its own citizens.

    Another line is that new entrant countries would be seen as a ‘poor relation’ and would not be as competitive when it comes to agriculture and other areas once they joined the EU.

    “What we’ve learned from our own elections is that disinformation does not stop after the elections, it continues constantly, and it adapts very quickly in terms of the narratives that it promotes, depending on the vulnerabilities that exist in each society that is targeted,” she added.

    “One very usual narrative targeting the EU is that all the land will be expropriated once Moldova joins the European Union, and that is meant to draw equal lines with how it used to be during the Soviet Union period for us, and that is meant to inflict fear that the EU is not there to support and protect its citizens, but it’s there to actually prey on them,” said Gherasimov.

    Ukrainian accession efforts labelled ‘futile’?

    Moldova knows about disinformation: a report in the New York Times last September said the Stimson Center – a research organisation in Washington – called the country “a testing ground for hybrid warfare operations” that “are likely to shape similar efforts” across Europe. 

    The same New York Times article referred to how, ahead of Moldova’s parliamentary election, social media platforms were flooded with fabricated posts, videos and websites, sometimes created using AI. 

    As outlined in this Euronews report, one post even impersonated the celebrity magazine OK! with a false story declaring “Moldovan president in celebrity sperm scandal!”. The concocted story, which incorrectly claimed that president Maia Sandu was buying sperm from gay celebrity donors to have a child, falsely used the name of a real reporter. 

    This demonstrates how disinformation frequently attempts to erode political reputations and steer voters towards particular political agendas. 

    Read more

    EU accession of Moldova and Ukraine is alternative to Nato, as Russia draws new Iron Curtain in Europe

    As with other forms of political disinformation, this takes many forms when it comes to EU accession, according to Vladyslav Lesyk, a journalist at Ukrainian media outlet Rubryka.

    “One of the primary Russian narratives regarding Ukraine’s EU accession is the claim that Ukraine’s efforts to join the Union are futile,” he said. 

    “For instance, Russian sources have spread fakes asserting that granting candidate status is a merely formal decision that offers no actual benefits. The functions of this narrative are to demoralise Ukrainian society and create the impression that the reforms required for EU membership are pointless,” he added.

    “Another Russian narrative suggests that joining the EU would mean Ukraine losing its sovereignty. This builds upon a broader Russian narrative, maintained since the start of the Russo-Ukrainian war in 2014, which portrays Ukraine as a state with an illegitimate government controlled by the West, specifically the EU and the US,” said Lesyk.

    Read more

    Wave of Russian sabotage attacks exposes counter-intelligence gaps on Nato’s eastern flank

    Disinformation is not new: EUvsDisinfo documents numerous past examples, including the infamous false story from 2014 of a boy allegedly being crucified by Ukrainian nationals in Slovyansk. This was cited to be part of a Kremlin-orchestrated campaign targeted at inciting hatred against Ukrainians.

    Ukraine has long articulated a desire to join the EU and the process is well underway. Since June 2022, Ukraine has official EU candidate status, with accession negotiations having formally started. Last September Ukraine successfully completed its screening process.

    Billions of euros in financial assistance have already been provided, while the EU has repeatedly affirmed its support for Ukraine’s independence, sovereignty and territorial integrity.

    The ‘burden’ narrative

    On the flip side, Lesyk said narratives spread in European countries lean into the idea of Ukraine becoming a “burden” on EU member states. 

    “In this context, Ukraine is presented as a poor and corrupt state whose accession would supposedly drain the European budget. A specific sub-narrative focuses on the negative impact of Ukrainian grain on European farming. Russians have been spreading the narrative of ‘harmful’ Ukrainian grain for several years to sow discord,” he said.

    Yet as this analysis from the European Policy Centre points out, Ukraine joining the EU would have very obvious benefits – including opening up the country’s energy potential to the EU, boosting EU food security, and providing ready trade in critical minerals.

    Lesyk said Telegram is the primary hub for disseminating these Russian narratives in Ukraine, as it allows for the use of anonymous channels and is one of the most popular sources of information in the country. 

    Regarding Moldova, media and fact-checking organisations have tracked a number of lines of attack regarding proposed EU membership, ranging from farms there closing due to Moldovan agricultural products not being in demand, to higher utility bills, and same-sex marriage. 

    These were analysed in depth by the website NewsMaker.md. Romanian fact-checking website Veridica has tracked numerous disinformation campaigns, including that Moldova could become a destination for migrants, could lose its statehood, or even be annexed by Romania.

    Read more

    [Interview] ‘Whenever we take pro-European political decisions, Russia cut or reduced gas supplies’. Moldova energy minister Dorin Junghietu on why Chișinău is betting on diversification

    Homegrown issues

    In Georgia, another country seemingly at a crossroads when it comes to possible EU membership, websites such as OC Media have tracked what they believe are coordinated Russian information operations in recent years.

    Salome Khvedelidze of OC Media said some of this runs on Facebook and other platforms. The International Society for Fair Elections and Democracy detailed material it described as “the dissemination of anti-Western, particularly anti-EU narratives”.

    Common themes include the EU being a threat to Georgian values, such as EU support for LGBTQ+ rights, the potential for EU interference in Georgian domestic affairs, and the idea of the EU and the US more broadly wanting to spark conflict.

    Read more

    Zelensky stalls on his EU promises to protect gay rights, even as Ukraine rushes through minority-languages law

    Since Russia’s war against Ukraine in 2022, Georgia has turned increasingly authoritarian, suspending EU accession talks and deepening its ties with Moscow.

    Recently, the ruling Georgian Dream party sought to ban the five main opposition parties – a move which is currently being fought in court. The European Parliament warned that this puts the country’s path towards EU membership at risk.

    According to Khvedelidze: “What makes Georgia different from Ukraine and Moldova, however, is where the main source of anti-EU propaganda actually comes from.”

    “In Ukraine and Moldova, disinformation about EU membership is driven by Russian proxies, Russia-backed/funded media, and certain political figures, while the governments themselves are pro-European,” she said.

    Arguably, it gives the impression of a message that is always changing but always the same. According to Cristina Gherasimov: “It adapts very quickly in terms of the narratives that it promotes, depending on the vulnerabilities that exist in each society that is targeted,” she added.

    It is not always straightforward to verify which narratives come directly from Russia and which originate elsewhere, but there is little doubt about Russia’s attitude towards the EU, and its history of spreading disinformation abroad.

    This article was written as part of a cross-border European journalistic collaboration within the framework of the EUNEIGHBOURS EAST programme. The original version was published by The Journal.

      <title>Microsoft outage shakes up companies, schools and local governments across US</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/13/microsoft-outage-shakes-up-companies-local-governments</link>
      <description><p>Local officials warn some services remain unavailable even as Outlook starts to resume normal operations after outage</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/live/2026/nov/13/microsoft-outage-down-today-live-update-outlook-teams-365-when-fixed-latest-status-cause-news">Microsoft outage – live updates</a></p></li></ul><p>The Microsoft Outlook outage has shaken up companies and local governments across the US that use its suite of email, calendar, video conferencing and cloud storage systems.</p><p>Even as Outlook started to resume normal operations Friday morning, local leaders from across the country, including in Miami, Maryland and Los Angeles, warned residents that certain staff or services were still unavailable due to the outage that started around 1pm ET on Thursday.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/13/microsoft-outage-shakes-up-companies-local-governments">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/13/faa-nationwide-ground-stop-flights</link>
      <description><p>Transportation secretary Sean Duffy says the airspace is now open and the problem has been identified</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/13/us-airports-flight-stoppage">Chaos at US airports as stoppage grinds travel plans to a halt</a></p></li><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/13/faa-ground-stop-flights-explained">What to know about the rare nationwide ground stop issued by the FAA</a></p></li></ul><p>Flights in the US have slowly started resuming after being grounded for several hours on Friday due to a major communications outage, but authorities have warned that a return to normal operations will take time.</p><p>The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) lifted a nationwide ground stop about four hours after it was declared on Friday afternoon, delaying or canceling more than 11,000 US flights, according to aviation tracker <a href="https://www.flightaware.com/live/cancelled/">FlightAware</a>, and throwing airports into sudden chaos.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/13/faa-nationwide-ground-stop-flights">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>Rallies are planned at more than US 40 campuses as workers seeking better pay and conditions decry stalled talks</p><p>Starbucks baristas, students, elected officials and allies are planning rallies at <a href="https://starbucksworkersunited.controlshift.app/events?link_id=2&amp;can_id=debd8d2ad19f005d15f9bbdff314d42a&amp;source=email-nov-12-day-of-action-for-starbucks-baristas&amp;email_referrer=email_3490793&amp;email_subject=nov-12-day-of-action-for-starbucks-baristas&amp;&amp;">over 40 college campuses</a> across the US on Thursday to support the Starbucks Workers United <a href="https://www.boycottstarbucks.net/">boycott campaign</a> as the union nears five years of deadlock with the company over contract negotiations.</p><p>Starbucks Workers United is <a href="https://sbworkersunited.org/what-were-fighting-for-updates-on-contract-bargaining/">seeking</a> better pay and stronger staffing levels, including a $17 an hour minimum wage for baristas and a minimum staffing of three workers per store.       <description><p>Sales of built units fell to 3.75m in October, down by 8.8% from last year, with mortgage rates at nearly three-year high</p><p>US existing home sales hit a 16-year low in October as buyers were driven away by high <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/money/mortgage-rates">mortgage rates</a> and rising inflation, according to new data released on Wednesday.</p><p>Sales of already built units dropped to 3.75m in October, down by 8.8% from last year, the National Association of Realtors (NAR) reported.       <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/11/democrats-election-medicaid-costs</link>
      <description><p>‘The post-election wish list is about to run into harsh fiscal reality: there is no money’</p><p>Is this an opportunity for a new America? As the Reagan revolution four decades ago launched US society down the path to low taxes and meager solidarity, perhaps the Republican bloodbath last week could turn US politics toward building a new social contract anchored on an aspiration to equitable prosperity.</p><p>One can sense the ambition of the bumper new crop of <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/democrats">Democrats</a> ushered to power last week, calling for support for programs for children and their parents; emphatically endorsing the long-held dream of Medicare for All. The project includes rolling back <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/donaldtrump">Donald Trump</a>’s cuts to Medicaid and food stamps, and restoring subsidies for health insurance under the Affordable Care Act that Republicans allowed to expire.       <description><p>Trump-appointed judge Jeffrey T Kuntz partially denies British broadcaster’s motion to dismiss over edit</p><p>Federal judge Jeffrey T Kuntz ruled on Tuesday that Donald Trump’s lawsuit against the BBC can proceed, denying in part the British broadcaster’s motion to dismiss the case.       <title>Farewell to Elon Musk’s Cybertruck. Has any car ever been more repellent? | Arwa Mahdawi</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2026/nov/11/farewell-cybertruck-elon-musk-car-repellent</link>
      <description><p>Safety campaigners have condemned it and owners have complained about it. Goodbye to a steel monstrosity seemingly designed by a five-year-old</p><p>Elon Musk is having a rough go of it, isn’t he? The world’s richest man spent almost half a billion dollars on the <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/04/elon-musk-midterm-spending-analysis">midterms</a> in a failed attempt to defend Republican control of government. Now the tech mogul, who moved from California to Texas to escape Democrats and regulations, finds himself in a newly blue state. He also finds himself the subject of an unflattering <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/sep/08/musk-review-epic-study-worlds-richest-most-banal-man-elon-film">documentary</a> and, if the Democrats follow through on threats to investigate him, could potentially be in a spot of legal bother.</p><p>And to top it all off? Musk’s beloved Cybertruck, the steel monstrosity that looks as if it were designed by a five-year-old, is <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/06/tesla-to-wind-down-cybertruck-production-as-elon-musk-focuses-on-robotics-and-ai">winding down production</a>. According to Musk, this isn’t because it’s an abject failure, but because he is channelling his energy into other things. “This is not a case of Cybertruck being unprofitable, as has been misreported by legacy media,” Musk <a href="https://x.com/elonmusk/status/2119691615774146614?a=pN3ISFVZZ-aU4_-TlJw&amp;s=20">tweeted</a> on Monday. “But rather that the opportunity cost of the complexity of Cybertruck is vastly outweighed by the value of incremental Cybercab production.” (The Cybercab is a two-passenger robotaxi.)</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2026/nov/11/farewell-cybertruck-elon-musk-car-repellent">Continue reading...</a></description>

<![CDATA[Irish Times Feeds]]>https://www.irishtimes.comSat, 14 Nov 2026 08:36:07 +0000en1hourly1<![CDATA[Gourmet Food Parlour opens first stand-alone restaurant in three years]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/14/new-chapter-for-gourmet-food-parlour-as-firm-opens-first-stand-alone-restaurant-in-three-years/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/14/new-chapter-for-gourmet-food-parlour-as-firm-opens-first-stand-alone-restaurant-in-three-years/Sat, 14 Nov 2026 05:00:00 +0000Gourmet Food Parlour – the independent restaurant brand that spans casual dining, coffee shops and catering services – is to open its 12th location later this month, marking the “beginning of a new chapter” for the company as its 20th year in business comes to a close.

Opening on November 23rd, this is the first stand-alone restaurant under the Gourmet Food Parlour name set up in nearly four years, although the company has established a footing under different names in the Brown Thomas and Arnotts department stores in Dublin’s city centre within that time frame.

Its newest location in 8th Lock – a residential and commercial development in Ashtown, Dublin 11, only a 15-minute walk along the Royal Canal from the green line Luas terminus at Broombridge – will host a 55-seater restaurant, open seven days a week and serve coffee, breakfast, brunch, lunch and dinner.

With the addition of at least 25 jobs at the new location, it brings Gourmet Food Parlour’s total employees to more than 345, according to the company.

Lorraine Heskin, who founded the business in 2006 and remains its chief executive, said this is the perfect way to round off an incredible 12 months for Gourmet Food Parlour.

“Customers can expect the same warm hospitality and high-quality food and drink they know and love at 8th Lock,” she said.

Gourmet Food Parlour has four stand-alone restaurants in Dublin – with locations in Dún Laoghaire, Malahide, Santry and Swords – as well as one in Galway’s Salthill neighbourhood and one in Dunshaughlin, Co Meath.

It also operates two outlets (Edition, a cafe, and Brown’s Brasserie, a restaurant) in Brown Thomas on Grafton Street as well as three (an Italian restaurant, a bistro and a cafe) in Arnotts on Henry Street.

In addition, the business has a catering services wing, with “a long-standing partnership with Dublin GAA” as well as League of Ireland champions Shamrock Rovers football club, and the Olympic Federation of Ireland.

]]>Alan Betson<![CDATA[Public service pay deal: What it means for someone on €30,000 or €60,000]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/politics/2026/11/14/public-service-pay-deal-what-it-means-for-a-special-needs-assistant-and-other-low-earners/https://www.irishtimes.com/politics/2026/11/14/public-service-pay-deal-what-it-means-for-a-special-needs-assistant-and-other-low-earners/Sat, 14 Nov 2026 06:00:00 +0000Thousands of special needs assistants (SNAs), clerical officers and other lower paid public sector workers are set to receive pay increases significantly beyond the 10.75 per cent headline figure in this week’s agreement between the Government and unions.

For anyone earning over €60,000 a year, that 10.75 per cent over two years and nine months will amount to 11.27 per cent when compounded.

For the very lowest paid public employees the uplift will exceed 18 per cent by March 2029. However, this example, provided by Government, of a newly recruited cleaner, is quite exceptional as the person would be one of the lowest earners in the entire public service.

An SNA with five years’ service will see their like-for-like income increase by 15.6 per cent over the term of the deal, while a newly recruited teacher, for example, will see a 12.75 per cent increase.

This assumes that they get the 1 per cent allocated for local bargaining, a mechanism for addressing sectoral or role-specific issues. This is not necessarily straight forward. All of the money may be allocated to a particular group of workers so they get significantly more than 1 per cent while others in the same sector get nothing. However, an even spread is assumed in the calculations given here.

Most employees in the public and Civil Service also benefit from annual increments during the early parts of their time in a particular role, an automatic annual increase linked to their growing experience.

In the case of SNAs, for instance, their pay would increase annually from €31,600 in year one to €47,300 in year 14 without any actual pay increases being received.

In the case of a principal officer on a higher scale, starting pay of €116,400 increases to €134,900 over five years. The number of increments depends on the role and these routinely provide substantial increases over time.

Such increments have been ignored for the purpose of these calculations, as have other elements of income, like allowances and overtime rates, many of which will be adjusted as a result of the new deal. In addition, figures have been rounded slightly for simplicity.

]]>Noreen M O Shea<![CDATA[How can Ireland afford to be so generous to public sector workers?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/opinion/2026/11/14/we-are-giving-out-pay-rises-not-because-productivity-is-up-but-because-we-have-money/https://www.irishtimes.com/opinion/2026/11/14/we-are-giving-out-pay-rises-not-because-productivity-is-up-but-because-we-have-money/Sat, 14 Nov 2026 05:00:00 +0000Did your Granny have a “good room”? In west Cork in the late 1970s, my Granny had a good room that was so good, I wasn’t good enough to go into it. In fact, none of my immediate family was. The good room was kept for people who were better than us: the parish priest, the solicitor or the local big Fine Gael farmer. After Mass, Granny would usher these better people into the good room, where my cousins and I lined up to meet them, drinking our MiWadi nervously from swanky Waterford glass goblets, terrified lest we drop a thing, not least our Tee Haitches. Once the good people were gone, the Waterford glass was carefully locked back in a press, not to be touched again until the next good room charade.

The aim was not to mortify the family. We were insecure about our position and let on to be richer than we were. The really posh people knew we were playing posh, and we knew that they knew we were putting it on, but everyone went along with the drama to avoid embarrassment.

No one made a Holy Show of themselves.

Good rooms are no longer a thing in Ireland, but the insecurity of good-room mentality pervades. These days the good people are no longer parish priests or local, Ford Granada-driving solicitors, but foreign leaders and dignitaries, the type of folk who arrived in Dublin last week. Our governing class still feels insecure alongside these cosmopolitan, multilingual continentals, and the last thing the lads could countenance was a messy public sector strike on the very day the national good room opened to our upscale visitors.

In terms of negotiating, this was the moment of maximum Government fragility and thus a maximum leverage point for the public sector workers. The unions struck a deal on Wednesday, and a truce was announced predawn, fittingly 106 years to the day of the first World War armistice. Face was saved, and the big event could pass off swimmingly – the good room won the day. But what about the economic and fiscal details of the latest deal? Once the black Mercs have swished the foreign grandees back to the airport, we will have to pick over the details to see who is on the hook for what.

The first thing to appreciate is that the Irish public sector is in overdrive mode, and has been for some time. The ultimate question is whether the expanded public sector offers the sort of value for money that would render legitimate a €5.2 billion pay deal that will deliver pay increases of 10.75 per cent over two years and nine months.

The growth of the public service is unambiguous. Annual expenditure has grown from roughly €15.3 billion in 1994 to €107 billion in 2025: a seven-fold nominal increase in three decades. Even allowing for inflation and population growth, the trajectory is striking. Spending nearly doubled between 2000 and 2010 (€26 billion to €61 billion), was reined in through austerity (falling to €54.6 billion by 2015). Spending has since exploded, up exactly 100 per cent in the decade to 2025. Health alone absorbed €25.8 billion in 2025 – more than the entire State budget only 25 years earlier in 2000 – while housing expenditure grew from €1.2 billion in 2015 to €9.3 billion by 2025, a near eight-fold increase in a single policy area within 10 years.

Lots of dough is being spent. But just how much is being spent per head? And how are we doing relative to other countries – are we spending more or less per head than the rest of Europe?

At first blush, things look good. When we stand back, we see that general Government expenditure in 2024 was 39.25 per cent of national income. Based on this, Ireland sits meaningfully below the European high-spenders – Finland (57.7 per cent), France (57.3 per cent) and Italy (50.4 per cent). Ireland is also below Spain (45.5 per cent) and the UK (44 per cent).

Public sector pay deal: What’s in it for me?

Public pay deal will be reviewed if economy deteriorates, Government and unions insist

But drill a bit deeper into the per-capita picture and a more nuanced and revealing story emerges. Last year, Ireland’s general Government expenditure was €133.5 billion, which is how much it costs to run our country of 5,308,039 people. We therefore spend about €25,198 per person. This means that Ireland’s Government actually spends more per person than even France – €25,198 versus €23,300 – and broadly comparable amounts to Finland (€24,200). We spend considerably more than Spain (€17,300) and Italy (€20,100), and somewhat less than the UK (€27,300).

Because our population is much younger, our unemployment levels much lower and our tax revenues more buoyant, this spending per head figure should set off alarm bells. It means Ireland is not spending anywhere near as efficiently as many of our neighbours. Given that productivity in the public service is so hard to measure, the notion that a young country – which should have far fewer demands on its health and welfare systems – is spending significantly more per head than older countries (which have far greater demands on the welfare state) means that productivity in the public sector in Ireland is lower than in other countries.

How can the State afford to be so generous to workers in the public sector without impoverishing other taxpayers? For context, 31.76 per cent of total current expenditure goes to public sector pay. Public sector employment rose from 301,000 in 2015 to 424,000 in 2026. Meanwhile, the average annual public sector pay is €56,496, compared to €40,200 in the private sector – a premium of approximately 40 per cent. If public sector workers are paid more, get more holidays, can’t be fired and have guaranteed pensions, something must give, surely? Are other workers shouldering this burden, and why are they not more pissed off?

The reason is simple: the money for the public sector pay rises is not coming from the tax paid by their neighbours, but from tax paid by foreign multinationals, which will amount to €34 billion this year, predicted to rise to €39 billion in 2027 and to €44.7 billion by 2030. In this scenario, the deal is comfortably affordable. The only question is how fragile this tax take is. We are giving out pay rises not because productivity has increased, but because we have the money, right now. It’s “kids with hands in the sweetie jar” time. Hardly the most confident look?

]]>Naoise Culhane<![CDATA[Apple’s iPhone Duo review: a great folding phone – but pricey]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/consumer-tech/review/2026/11/14/apples-iphone-duo-review-a-great-folding-phone-but-pricey/https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/consumer-tech/review/2026/11/14/apples-iphone-duo-review-a-great-folding-phone-but-pricey/Sat, 14 Nov 2026 06:00:00 +0000There is a lot to like about the iPhone Duo. Some of that hasn’t been for the right reasons – reports of failing screens and stock shortages, for example – but on the whole, the opinion seems to be that Apple has done something good here, even if it is eye-wateringly expensive.

Foldable phones have always been a great idea in theory; the reality has often fallen far short. The early days were marred by screens that peeled or a less than stellar multitasking experience. Later models struggled to find the perfect size that would make the folded version as good as a standard smartphone for everyday tasks while accommodating a folding screen without making the whole thing too thick.

The iPhone Duo manages to neatly sidestep that problem. At less than half an inch thick when closed, the phone is not far off the iPhone 18 Pro, which comes in at 0.34 inches. It weighs in at 254 grams, a little heavier than the iPhone 18 Pro’s 211 grams.

The closest comparison is with the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8, a passport-sized folding phone that manages to bridge the gap between the phone that people want and the one they can actually use.

The nano texture on the inner display certainly disguises the crease, especially when content is on the screen, although nothing can eliminate it entirely. The crease is far less visible than anything I’ve seen on any other foldable phone, and it will be interesting to see how that holds up over the course of a year or two with the product.

It supports Apple Pencil too – the USB C version – so you can use it to take notes, draw or just as a smart stylus.

But there are downsides. The main sacrifice comes with the camera, which only has the wide and ultrawide lens, leaving the telephoto lens out. If you are coming from the standard iPhone, that will not be a big issue as the more powerful telephoto lens has been primarily on the iPhone’s Pro models.

The front-facing camera is only 12 megapixels instead of the 18 that we have come to expect, although it retains the centre stage capabilities that keep you in the middle of the frame. The downgrade is small, admittedly; you also get the under-display FaceTime camera on the inner display, which is only really useful for video calls and is of much lower quality.

Can a focus on simplicity give Google’s Fitbit the Edge?

Apple has built in extras for the camera such as KidCue – similar to Google’s Made You Look feature – that displays an animation of Snoopy on the outer screen when you are using the camera with the display folded out to keep a child’s attention. There is also Smart Take, which will detect when everyone is looking at the camera and then snap a shot.

But the camera doesn’t use the inner display to its fullest, sticking with the same layout as every other iPhone despite the extra screen real estate. And the Duo lacks some of the more advanced features of the 18 Pro, including the ability to shoot RAW format and the pro controls.

So the Duo gives, and the Duo takes away. Multitasking with some apps works well, pinning two apps side by side. But there are others that would do well from a redesign to take advantage of the extra space that the Duo offers, either in how they are displayed (Gmail) or just simply by making them fit the screen and ditch the black bars (Duolingo).

You can get around this a bit by using multitasking, where you have an app open in each half of the Duo’s folded out display. For example, I like to have Google Docs and Safari open side by side. Once I open Docs and drag it to one side of the screen, I can open Safari in Split View, and the phone will remember that pairing for as long as I need it to.

Apple iPhone 18 Pro review: New smartphone makes advances but feels like a place holder

What you also don’t get is FaceID; the iPhone Duo uses TouchID instead to log you in to websites or unlock payments. Again, not a huge deal, but when you have been used to the seamless Face ID process, TouchID is a bit of a throwback.

Some of these issues can be resolved with software updated, including the app support, the decision for which rests with the developers. But it makes using the phone a little less pleasant.

Good

When it comes to design, the iPhone Duo is almost perfect. Closed it is the ideal size for one-handed use; open you get almost as much space as an iPad Mini.

Battery life was better than I expected, with the batteries in both sides of the fold giving me most of a day out of the device while using the outer display for most tasks. That inner display can really suck up the battery, though.

Multitasking is very useful. I can run two apps side by side, and the Duo will remember the app pairing for the future.

Bad

The front display looks great but when it comes to apps, there is a lot of wasted space. There are a lot of apps that don’t make full use of the iPhone Duo’s larger inner screen, including its own camera app. Think thick black bars everywhere.

You can’t mention the downsides without talking about the price. At almost €2,400, the iPhone Duo is out of reach of many consumers. Even with a contract, you are talking about a sizeable investment.

Everything else

The under-screen camera is fine, but should only be used for video calling. And invest in a good case, which should also help with the impact of the camera bump on the back of the phone.

Verdict

As a first attempt at a folding phone, Apple has learned from the mistakes of its rivals. The good outweighs a few flaws, but the price will be a stumbling block for most would-be Duo owners.

]]>Bryan O'Brien<![CDATA[Microsoft outage: What happened and what does it say about online services?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/2026/11/13/microsoft-outage-what-happened-and-when-will-it-be-fixed/https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/2026/11/13/microsoft-outage-what-happened-and-when-will-it-be-fixed/Fri, 13 Nov 2026 18:27:12 +0000Millions of people were unable to access their emails, Teams chats or meetings on Thursday night and Friday after a Microsoft 365 outage brought down services across the globe.

The outage was into its second day on Friday, though Microsoft said it was seeing “encouraging recovery progress in Europe”. It affected businesses, government agencies and even Microsoft employees all over the world.

The Health Service Executive said it had been affected by the global Microsoft outage, with emails not being transmitted.

Those also reporting issues have included the US House of Representatives, an Australian spy agency, airlines in India, European government agencies, and police services, ambulances and hospitals in the UK.

Microsoft is still investigating the cause of the outage, which it has said is not a cyberattack but a configuration error.

Experts say that the outage has laid bare the dangerous dependence of countries on a few US tech companies.

What happened and why?

On Thursday, the outage website Down Detector showed an increase in users reporting issues with Microsoft 365, the assembly of cloud software that includes Teams, Word, Excel, PowerPoint and Outlook.

By Friday morning, Microsoft had narrowed down most of the problems to Microsoft Exchange, the email service behind Outlook. Teams meetings and chats had returned to service.

On Friday afternoon, Microsoft said there was “encouraging recovery progress in Europe”, improvements in North America and Asia Pacific, and Japan was “stable”.

What caused the disruption?

Microsoft has said that this was not the result of a cyberattack, though suspicions were high because of several cyberattacks that have hit organisations in Europe in recent weeks. So far, the problem appeared to be a configuration update that resulted in some servers becoming overloaded and taken offline, Microsoft indicated.

When the company attempted to apply a fix, servers that had come back online again became unresponsive when traffic began returning to them.

As some servers went down, traffic was funnelled on to the remaining servers, causing traffic problems for those remaining online.

More details are likely to emerge over the coming weeks. “We don’t know what actually went wrong, and that will take weeks to discover,” said Steven Murdoch, a professor of security engineering at University College London. “The people who are working on it are too busy fixing to understand or report on the cause.”

Why has Microsoft 365 been down for so long?

An outage that runs for so long for a service as critical as Microsoft 365 is unusual. The company has not said why it has lasted this long, but a clue might be in its updates: as servers returned to being unresponsive after being fixed, engineers had to work through alternative solutions, taking longer than expected to get servers back up and running.

What does the incident say about our reliance on online services?

Experts have said that outages such as this underscored the world’s reliance on cloud services provided by a few large US tech companies – Amazon, Google and Microsoft. This reliance has been a growing source of unease through each high-profile outage.

It has grown more pronounced because of the hostility of the Trump administration towards Europe, which has prompted some governments to consider alternatives to US software.

As the name Microsoft 365 implies, the world has quickly become accustomed to online services being available 24/7. Given that software is no longer solely downloaded to individual PCs but is also stored on a server owned by a company, outages such as this will happen. Most of the time they are brief, but sometimes they are not.

Outages in recent years from telecommunications providers, from the PHP incident to the CrowdStrike incident, show just how varied the sources and causes of a large outage can be.

There are many different pieces of the puzzle keeping services online – but the effect of one of those services going down is much greater than it ever has been.

Mark Gregory, an associate professor at Australia’s RMIT University, said it was important for organisations to thoroughly test updates before rolling them out to the live network.

That was in addition to the extra security testing companies must carry out to ensure their services are protected from threat actors armed with AI tools that can find vulnerabilities quicker than ever before.

Should we have backup options when services go down?

Gregory said companies that relied on services such as Microsoft 365 should have backup options such as Google’s Gmail in the event of an outage. Others have suggested the free and open-source Office alternative LibreOffice.

Around the world, it has become increasingly clear that many companies – and government services – do not have good backups, with businesses resorting to faxes and phones. – Guardian
