]]>Patrick Bolger<![CDATA[Take the time to prepare for retirement ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/13/take-the-time-to-prepare-for-retirement/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/13/take-the-time-to-prepare-for-retirement/Fri, 13 Nov 2026 14:29:54 +0000Getting your finances straight, prioritising your mental and physical health and finding enjoyable ways to spend your time are key to a happy retirement

If you’ve spent years working for the boss from hell, then it’s likely retirement can’t come fast enough. But if your working life has been tolerable or, better still, enjoyable and fulfilling, calling it a day can come with mixed emotions.

We’ve all come across energetic retirees with a bucket list as long as your arm, but not everyone views this pivot in their lives in the same light. Worries about health, having enough money to live on or caring for others can peak around this time.

And there’s always the potential for family friction if adult children assume that their recently retired parent has nothing else to do but look after their grandchildren.

Retirement is a huge change for the retiree but it also triggers upheaval for the whole family, especially for a partner used to having the house to themselves for most of the day. Suddenly having to share 24/7 with someone who mopes around the place or has no interests or hobbies can be a huge strain. It is a possible explanation for a spike in separations among those in their 60s.

In an ideal world, those nearing retirement age would begin planning ahead. A good place to start is by sorting out your immediate finances. (Your pension is a whole different ball game that needs to be dealt with separately.)

Once retired, you may have less money to spend day to day which makes it important to decide what your financial priorities are. Do you want to spend your money on travel, on your home or hobbies or helping out the family?

Incomes typically fall post-retirement so while you are still bringing in a regular wage it is worth dealing with outstanding debts such as loans and credit cards.

If you have multiple loans and/or several credit cards with outstanding balances, try to pay off what you can before you retire and consider consolidation to save on fees and card and interest charges.

Some people like to have two credit cards for emergencies. However, it is best to stick to one as your main card for buying and become vigilant about paying off the balance each month, bearing in mind that there will be no monthly salary to cover the cost if you overspend or let the interest build up.

Check with your bank if they offer any perks to older customers, such as an account with reduced fees and charges. These accounts are usually available for those aged 66 or over.

Some banks also offer financial advice and planning for older customers but, like a lot of things in life, if you want it you have to ask for it.

Retirement can be an opportunity to reinvent yourself and to do the things you’ve always wanted to do. It can also provide more time for grandchildren which can be good or not so good depending on the circumstances.

The sentiment often expressed by grandparents is that while they love their grandchildren, it’s great to be able to hand them back to their parents. That is something that has become a lot trickier with childcare costs and places at a premium.

As a consequence, some adult children expect parents to step up for child-minding duties. Declining to do so or putting conditions in place can go down badly at times. These are potentially troubled waters so it may be worth thinking about how much babysitting you want to do and to be clear in your own mind about the boundaries before the time arrives.

Otherwise what starts out as a casual or stopgap arrangement can morph into a full-time commitment that is hard to get out of.

One solution is not to be permanently available. That’s where getting stuck into new hobbies or activities comes in. Volunteering, a new sport, a hobby, taking up an academic course or joining a choir or sea swimming group are all sociable ways of spending time that help foster good mental health and maintain the interpersonal connections that inevitably diminish when you’re no longer in full-time employment.

One often hears retirees opining that they’d prefer to watch paint drying than going hillwalking or playing bridge. But there are many other options if you dig a little. For example, rug tufting (very satisfactory as you do it with a gun and the pieces take shape fast) or joining a percussion group. Rhythm and beat are very therapeutic, and percussion includes a myriad of styles from African djembe to Japanese style drumming to learning to play the bodhrán.

Making stained glass pieces seems to suit those who like precision and wielding a soldering iron, while fused glass is a wide-open form of expression where creativity can run wild. Add to that activities like stone cutting, willow sculpture, axe throwing and Mahjong, and you are still only scratching the surface of what’s out there.

Health

Having ticked the boxes marked “money” and “filling time”, the third pillar is health and what you should do to mind it.

There is no shortage of health gurus telling us how to eat and how to exercise and it can be easy to get overwhelmed by all the noise. But strip it back and it’s pretty simple.

Move as much as possible, stay hydrated to avoid urinary tract infections, maintain social contacts and eat to preserve muscle strength, bone density and a good gut microbiome. Appetite can reduce with age so it’s important to keep a steady calorie intake to maintain energy levels and feel well.

As we get older, the combination of underlying medical conditions and natural ageing can disrupt the systems that normally keep us upright. Balance problems are one of the main fall risks for older adults.

A bad fall can be life changing which is why it’s worth incorporating exercises to maintain balance into your daily routine. These exercises require no special equipment and even 10 minutes a day has been shown to cut the risk of a fall. One of the simplest is calf raises which can be done at the worktop while you’re waiting for the kettle to boil.

ExWell Medical is a not for profit social enterprise that runs medically supervised exercise classes (and online health information sessions) for older people in the community. It was started by Dr Noel McCaffrey in 2019 and the aim is to keep people moving even if they are living with health issues, debilitating conditions or recovering from serious illnesses such as cardiac events or cancer.

The classes are pitched at different fitness levels and some can be done seated. To join a group, you must be referred by a medical practitioner. Full details of the locations of ExWell’s classes are on the organisation’s website.

For those who feel they would benefit from a more formal introduction to what retirement may bring, the Retirement Planning Council of Ireland runs year-round courses for those coming up to retirement. You can pay up and go as a private individual or your company may be willing to foot the bill so it’s worth checking that with HR.

The courses cover areas such as financial readiness, pensions, legal and lifestyle transitions.

You can contact us at OnTheMoney@irishtimes.com with personal finance questions you would like to see us address. If you missed last week’s newsletter, you can read it here.

]]>Daniel Balakov<![CDATA[Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes turns herself in for 11-year prison term following fraud saga]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2023/05/30/theranos-founder-elizabeth-holmes-turns-herself-in-for-11-year-prison-term-following-fraud-saga/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2023/05/30/theranos-founder-elizabeth-holmes-turns-herself-in-for-11-year-prison-term-following-fraud-saga/Tue, 30 May 2023 19:07:23 +0000Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes has turned herself in for an 11-year prison sentence, marking a final chapter in a years-long fraud saga that riveted Silicon Valley.

]]>Julia Demaree Nikhinson<![CDATA[Public sector pay deal: did the Government capitulate or did unions settle for too little?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/11/13/public-sector-pay-deal-did-the-government-capitulate-or-did-unions-settle-for-too-little/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/11/13/public-sector-pay-deal-did-the-government-capitulate-or-did-unions-settle-for-too-little/Fri, 13 Nov 2026 06:00:01 +0000There was always going to be a deal. The question was where both sides would settle. We got the answer in the early hours of Wednesday morning.

A 10.75 per cent pay hike spread out over 33 months (to March 2029) at a cost of €5.2 billion to the exchequer.

The latest round of public sector pay negotiations was unusually fraught by Irish standards but not by European standards, where industrial relations have been souring for months on the back of persistent inflation.

A fierce standoff over cost of living and pension reform has paralysed France.

If you believe one side of the commentariat, the Government capitulated at the last minute to avoid the mayhem of another one-day national strike coinciding with Ireland’s hosting of the EU summit.

But to evaluate the true merits of the deal, you need to go back to the starting point for negotiations.

Government and unions held exploratory talks in early July, but the real discussions didn’t start until October under the auspices of the Workplace Relations Commission.

On the table was the Central Bank’s latest quarterly bulletin, published the previous month, containing the bank’s inflation forecasts for 2026, 2027 and 2028 (3.4 per cent; 3.1 per cent; 2 per cent).

The forecast for 2027 had been upgraded by nearly half a percentage point since the summer, reflecting the deteriorating economic backdrop.

Public sector pay deal: What’s in it for me?

Inflation-proofing wages was the primary objective of unions.

As the negotiations progressed, the Central Bank’s inflation forecasts began to look shaky.

Oil prices were on the march again. Speculation was rife that the US and Israel were about to attack Iran again.

Unions began coming up with their own estimates of future price growth based on the latest readouts. The fear was that they would sign up to pay rises that would later be crushed by inflation.

The Government’s initial offer of a cumulative 7.75 per cent pay hike didn’t even cover the conservative inflation forecasts, hence the deadlock.

The deal eventually struck gives public sector workers in higher-income brackets a pay bump of 4.6 per cent next year (when the backdated element is included), followed by 3.1 per cent in 2028 and 3.2 per cent in 2029. Lower-paid workers, those earning less than €50,000, will get bigger pay increases.

Based on the current inflationary outlook, which has improved since the US midterm elections, this will give public sector workers modest but real wage increases.

Another benchmark for both sides to consider was the expected rise in wages in the private sector.

The Government’s recent economic and fiscal outlook, published alongside last month’s budget, forecasts that wages across the economy – which is mainly private sector – would rise by 4.1 per cent in 2027 and by 3.7 per cent in 2028 and 2029. The public sector deal is roughly comparable.

The deal includes a review clause that can be triggered by either side if economic conditions or inflation rates change “significantly”, reflecting the fact that both unions and Government are unsure about the economic outlook. Not an unreasonable position given the last five years.

Jack Chambers warns public sector pay deal could be reviewed if economy contracts

The Government typically defends pay deals as a means of preventing industrial unrest, ensuring continuity of service and pay predictability.

There is, however, a big unknown for Government.

The Department of Finance’s latest expenditure outlook report says Budget 2027 includes “the costs associated with the recruitment of circa 7,000 additional [public sector] staff”.

But public sector employment has grown by 85,000 since 2019, which equates to an average of 12,000 a year.

There is also nothing in the report or other reports about the additional staff (nurses, teachers, gardaí) needed or expected after 2027.

The Government’s €5.2 billion costing is therefore something of a shot in the dark.

In its back pocket, however, is the promise of more corporation tax, the exchequer’s golden goose. Receipts from the business tax are expected to climb to €45 billion by 2030.

But weaving more day-to-day spending around risky tax receipts is a gamble the Government has been repeatedly advised against.

The Irish Times view on the public pay deal: the Government pays up for peace

The draft deal (it still has to be ratified by unions) will cost the Government an estimated €2 billion next year, which means Budget 2027, which allocates €1.2 billion for the deal, is already out of date. €800 million out of date.

They say the definition of a good deal is when both sides walk away thinking they could have done better. That’s probably not the case here.

Both sides will sell it as a good deal in the context of the economic backdrop. But there are big unknowns to do with inflation and cost.

Several of its lending platforms advanced loans in recent years to a fund managed by Mel Sutcliffe’s Quanta Capital and property ventures that were linked to Press Up co-founders Paddy McKillen jnr and Matt Ryan.

Newly published financial statements by five firms controlled by Relm Finance show their total balance of outstanding loans was €609.9 million at the end of 2025, down from €698.9 million the previous year.

The firms recorded €207.4 million of loan repayments in the year, and €115.6 million of new drawdowns.

Three of Relm’s vehicles also reported a combined €198.9 million of loans as past their redemption dates at the end of 2025, up from €174.9 million at the end of 2024. An additional €12.5 million in interest is owed on the loans past redemption.

Relm Loan Opportunities 3 reported the largest overdue balance at €78.1 million, while Relm Loan Opportunities 2 said all of the €59.9 million of loans it issued were now past their repayment dates. Accounts for Relm Loan Opportunities 4 said €60.9 million of its €69.9 million portfolio was past the redemption date.

Each of the three firms, which did not identify the borrowers linked to the overdue loans, said they have “taken steps” to recover the outstanding balance.

In the past two years, these Relm Finance lending vehicles have appointed receivers to firms controlling notable Irish office, hotel and hospitality properties.

In November 2024, the lender appointed receivers over 27 properties, including the building housing the Israeli embassy on Shelbourne Road in Ballsbridge and 58 Northumberland Road, linked to Sutcliffe’s Quanta Capital.

The properties were controlled through a sub-fund of Goldstein Property ICAV, an investment vehicle managed by Quanta Capital, which subsequently sued Relm Loan Opportunities 2, 3 and 4 in February.

Goldstein sought an injunction to prevent the receivers from selling the properties and disputed the amount needed to redeem the loans. The courts refused the application, and Goldstein later sought an appeal in July.

In March 2025, both Relm Loan Opportunities 3 and Relm Loan Opportunities 4 appointed receivers over close to a dozen real estate assets that were linked to McKillen jnr at the time.

Only the real estate assets, and not the businesses trading from the premises, were part of the process initiated by Relm Finance. Properties involved in the receivership included the building that previously housed Topshop on St Stephen’s Green in Dublin, Ashton’s in Clonskeagh and The Foxhunter in Lucan.

The receivers subsequently took control of some Dublin office buildings used by Paddy McKillen jnr’s Grafter business, and the businessman sued them, alleging they did so unlawfully.

In January 2026, the High Court was told that five sets of proceedings arising from the receiverships had been resolved. The parties agreed that the cases, including actions brought by McKillen jnr and several companies linked to him, would be struck out.

Some of the assets linked to McKillen jnr that were placed into receivership, including The Butler Arms Hotel in Co Kerry and a building in Temple Bar that previously housed the Vintage Cocktail Club, have been sold by receivers appointed by Relm Finance.

The accounts for the three Relm Finance firms, which reported a combined €198.9 million of loans past repayment dates, said that post year-end €13.7 million of the amount owed was received.

Spokespeople for Relm Finance and Sutcliffe declined to comment. A spokeswoman for McKillen jnr did not respond to a request for comment.

She is slightly sceptical about introducing AI into the business: the new technology can impact adherence to the EU’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and, given the sensitivity of much of the app’s health data, this can go south quite quickly.

At Web Summit, at least, she was in good company – with 115 Irish start-ups exhibiting at the tech fair. This is the highest number in its history, according to the organisers.

“In 2017, two Irish start-ups exhibited at Web Summit in Lisbon. This year there are more than 110. That’s crazy growth,” chief executive Paddy Cosgrave said in a statement.

The event hosted its largest ever Chinese delegation and had a difficult-to-ignore presence of humanoid robots. As was to be expected, many of the event’s discussion panels and start-up exhibitions had an increased focus on harnessing AI for business innovation.

That appeared to be less of a focus at the Irish start-ups centre – although Jonathan Browne seemed in his element on the topic.

“That’s exactly what we’re focused on, enabling AI in business,” he says as the chief executive of Octoglo, an agentic AI start-up that enables businesses to centralise their AI use within back-end systems through a single platform.

“Our big claim to fame is that it’s AI to the desk in less than 15 minutes – no projects, no lengthy roll-out, no budget requirements,” he says.

“The big thing really is to just get started with AI – sometimes these new frontiers can seem daunting, but I think the main concept for me is to get started and get started quickly. Ultimately, what we’re trying to do is to give people more time to focus on their business.”

The company is 18 months in the making and has already reached “commercial-grade platforms”, according to Browne, “so it’s ready to go”.

Browne continues to run a separate business alongside this venture. He started that business back in 2010, which was “the last time I certainly didn’t have this parachute there with me”, he says, referring to his current, more secure employment. He attended Web Summit more than 10 years ago, when it was held in Dublin’s RDS.

“Look at the scale of it – it’s large,” he says of the tech conference’s current status in Lisbon. “There’s a great mix of people, really interesting conversations, a lot of innovation going on – it’s great..

When The Irish Times visited the stands hosting Irish startups, there was a dizzying sense of excitement among them. A sense of camaraderie too, having been on their feet all day together.

“The Irish start-ups exhibiting at Web Summit demonstrate the depth of innovation and international ambition from our early-stage company portfolio,” says Anna-Marie Turley, the head of enterprise solutions at Enterprise Ireland, which helped finance the appearance of some Irish startups at Web Summit.

“Collectively, 18 of the participating companies are seeking nearly €30 million in investment to accelerate their growth,” she adds. “Web Summit provides an important opportunity to connect with international investors, customers and partners, and Enterprise Ireland is committed to supporting these ambitious companies as they scale into global markets.”

However, the Irish start-up ecosystem faces challenges at home in attracting funding. Venture capital funding for SMEs in Ireland fell by 10 per cent in the first half of this year, according to the Irish Venture Capital Association (IVCA), with foreign investment accounting for 82 per cent of all the funds during that time.

“These levels are flashing red warning signals as they represent some of the highest on record and emphasise our over-exposure to overseas investors,” says Richard Watson, IVCA’s chairman.

Many of the Irish startups at Web Summit will be vying for that capital. Placed near the larger German and Czech start-up exhibitions, and right next to a seemingly never-ending queue for a coffee stand, the exhibiting companies were in prime position for caffeine-induced enthusiasm from fellow conference-goers.

Far from the fanfare of Web Summit, however, in a rural Co Mayo village, the shared pitch of two local GAA and football clubs has fallen into disrepair, with weeds spurting from the soil and grass too tall to cut.

Aidan Gaughan once painted its markings – the white lines that define the boundaries of the pitch – but not any more.

Only 200 or so people live in Bonniconlon, a classic one-road town some 10km from Ballina but actually closer to the border with Co Sligo. This small population has led its local football club through times of struggle, attracting enough volunteers and players to get by. .

Somewhat accepting the limitations that come with operating multiple sports teams to service such a small population, Gaughan has put his bachelor’s degree in engineering and master’s in robotics to good use in Nerium Technology.

“We manufacture autonomous robots that mark sports pitches – basically, the robot uses GPS and satellite information to go around and spray white lines of sports fields,” he says, offering up a well-practised elevator pitch.

While it may sound like a minor necessity, Gaughan thinks it can have a practical and personal benefit. “Every weekend, I used to have to line my local team’s pitch, as my dad had done for years before me. And one time in particular, I was away and a team-mate was meant to line it for me.

“When we turned up to play the game on Sunday, there were no marks on the pitch – so I had to run around all my team-mates while they were warming up to get it done before kick off,” he says, adding that “most amateur clubs depend on volunteers” for everyday tasks yet “the numbers are declining” amid an ageing population.

“I just thought surely in this day and age, there has to be a robot to do that for you.”

Sure enough, there was. The only problem was its price point. “It cost €35,000 to purchase”, Gaughan says, “crazy money”. Like so many others presenting at Web Summit in Lisbon this week, his start-up began as a fix to a problem in his own life – his solution will come to the market for around €5,000, he says.

Gaughan was studying for a bachelor’s degree in engineering at Sligo Atlantic University at the time, and thought he could “make something for less than that, that’s more affordable for your average club”. It was during his master’s in robotics in Bath University, however, that the project took off when the central idea of his dissertation became Nerium Technology’s first prototype.

Yet unlike many of his fellow attendees, Gaughan does not see his start-up depending on AI-powered technologies in the future: “It’s probably even more simple than that – it doesn’t need any AI . . . it’s actually quite a simple idea, because it uses satellites to operate through GPS”.

As the venture progressed, so too did the commitment it required. He left his full-time job a little more than a year ago to go all-in on his start-up. “My family were kind of wondering what I was doing when I left to go at this, but I just wanted to give it my best shot,” he adds.

Was it a leap of faith? “Big time,” Gaughan says.

But is it worth the risk? “Absolutely. It’s trying to make technology accessible for everyone.”

]]>Chris Maddaloni<![CDATA[Irish reunification will be costly - here are the key decisions which will decide the size of the bill]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/12/the-key-political-choices-that-will-determine-the-cost-of-irish-reunification/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/12/the-key-political-choices-that-will-determine-the-cost-of-irish-reunification/Thu, 12 Nov 2026 14:41:03 +0000The economics of a united Ireland has been a disputed territory for years, with analysis ranging from claims of large gains to significant costs. How do we make sense of this?

A new analysis from Prof Stephen Kinsella of the University of Limerick – The Economics of Reunification – published by Fine Gael as part of its ardfheis initiative on the topic, provides a vital guide through the arguments.

It shows, above all, two things. One is that the costs depend crucially on what model is chosen, how it is implemented and crucial negotiations with the UK on the issue of pensions and debt. And second, that the long-term growth performance of Northern Ireland will be crucial in determining the economics of reunification and whether it can be financed.

There is no one answer to the question of what a united Ireland would cost. It all depends. And this underlines the vital role of planning and preparation.

Kinsella, who is an adviser to Tánaiste Simon Harris, draws on a range of previous work, much of it undertaken post-Brexit. He estimates that the first-year cost of reunification ranges from about €3 billion to €25 billion.

This is obviously a huge range. But this is where the story lies. As the assumptions and political choices change, so do the potential costs.

Kinsella frames the issue of the economics of the reunification debate around two questions. The first is who should pay which parts of the difference between Northern Ireland’s income and its expenditure. The second is what structures can be put in place to improve convergence between income and productivity levels in Northern Ireland and the Republic.

Disposable income per household is 13 per cent higher south of the Border, and the FDI model has boosted the Republic’s economy and its public finances. In contrast, the North has a net fiscal deficit of €17 billion, funded by the UK exchequer. This does not transfer automatically to the costs of reunification, but it is important nonetheless.

In a best-case scenario, if the UK agreed to take on the historic cost of the North’s pensions bill and the debt interest on the part of the UK’s national debt which would be attributed to Northern Ireland, then much of the €17 billion deficit would fall away.

Kinsella assumes some additional costs would accrue to the Republic from investment and running a separate administration if a federal model was chosen. This is one of a range of integration models in the paper, which also includes what he calls a “managed integration” plan – involving phased harmonisation in areas such as pay and welfare rates over 15 years – and a costly scenario that harmonises everything at once.

This variety of political decisions on what form unification would take and who picks up various bills leaves a potential matrix of costs not only, of course, in year one but for many years into the future. Bringing public pay and welfare rates in the North up to the Republic’s level, for example, would be a hugely expensive exercise.

The most important decisions are:

The pensions and debt issue

What happens to the accrued pension liabilities of Northern Ireland public servants and those who qualify for a state pension has been a key difference over the years between those taking an optimistic and pessimistic view of the economic benefits of reunification. Added to this is the interest on the part of the UK national debt, allocated to Northern Ireland in relation to its size within the UK.

Together these sum to close to €10 billion of the €17 billion annual UK estimate of the Northern Ireland deficit.

Pay convergence

Partly relying on what model of unification is chosen, it is clear that, as Kinsella puts it, “a nurse, teacher or civil servant in Belfast would expect the same pay as one in Dublin and a pensioner or jobseeker in Derry would expect the same weekly payment as one in Cork.” This would cost between €2.3 billion and €12.4 billion on day one, depending on how the gaps are measured, according to the report.

Northern envy at Republic pay rates

Huge decisions would lie ahead in this area and on the wider issue of how – or whether – public services would be integrated. Savings might be expected here from unified structures, but this would mean job losses, and Kinsella warns that the gains might be modest enough.

The model chosen

Choosing between the different possible models for reunification also has an impact on the economics.

A key message is that trying to unite the two economies in an unplanned rush is potentially very expensive and would require strong growth in Northern Ireland to make the finances add up in any fashion.

So-called managed integration over 15 years would still carry a high cost, on his calculations. Extra investment needed to increase productivity in the North would also need to be factored in.

As Kinsella says in his conclusions, a key message is that political choices will drive the cost of reunification – “the price depends far more on decisions made by policymakers than on any fixed bill”. The pensions and debt issues are vital in the short term, while over time closing the pay and welfare gap is crucial.

In any scenario, the financing is complicated, requiring significant borrowing even if there is financial assistance from the UK or even the European Union (where other member states might look askance at the idea given the public-finance constraints they face).

For the financing to work, growth becomes vital. Northern Ireland has averaged 1.3 per cent a year GDP growth since the early 2000s. Under a managed transition scenario, this would need to rise – depending on the assumptions – to between 3 per cent and 4.7 per cent on average each year to underpin a funding model.

Kinsella concludes that “this is a high bar, but it is possible”. Other assumptions might lower the growth targets a bit – again showing the importance of the key decisions.

A key conclusion from reading the report is that the potential financial implications for the Republic and its citizens are significant. Kinsella points to a range of potential costs per head in the Republic, which runs from €650 in year one to more than €2,600, with ongoing significant costs in future years.

Cross-Border tax rules putting off employers and workers, says report

Ireland’s public finances give it leeway to fund reunification, but this still carries costs. “However the costs are shared,” Kinsella writes, “someone has to pay them year by year.”

Like previous work by economists John FitzGerald and Edgar Morgenroth, the report points to the investment needs of Northern Ireland in areas such as education and skills, infrastructure and other measures to boost productivity.

There are potential gains from unification, too, as – for example – corporate taxes are cut in the North, encouraging inward investment, and new trade opportunities open up as the Irish Border disappears and Northern Ireland becomes a full part of the EU.

The extent of the resulting dynamic is hugely difficult to model with any confidence, but the North’s lacklustre economic performance compared with the Republic does point to some potential gains.

As the report concludes, whether reunification happens is a political and constitutional question. But the economics will be vital, and the report again underlines the complexity of the task and the huge preparations which would be required.

]]>www.dwalshphoto.ie 0872672033<![CDATA[Who could run Nvidia after Jensen Huang’s ousting following report of a second affair?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/11/12/who-could-run-nvidia-if-jensen-huang-is-ousted/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/11/12/who-could-run-nvidia-if-jensen-huang-is-ousted/Thu, 12 Nov 2026 10:20:12 +0000Jensen Huang is such a towering figure at Nvidia that his extramarital affairs – with a suspected Chinese spy and reportedly with a colleague – has left the world’s most valuable chipmaker with what could be the world’s biggest corporate succession problem after his resignation on Thursday.

Talamh Beo suggests that to qualify for a basic income, food producers would need to have a minimum annual turnover of €8,000, engage in agroecological farming practices, be certified organic or be in conversion to organic farming and be selling at least 70 per cent of their produce locally through markets, direct to customers or to local restaurants.

The Irish Times view on food security: time is short to avert a crisis

The backdrop to this initiative is growing concern that food security – the availability of essential food supplies – is threatened by geopolitical tensions and extreme weather events affecting food harvests across the world.

So-called “environmental externalities” – degradation of water, soil and air from intensive agricultural practices – and the concomitant greenhouse gas emissions are key issues of concern to Talamh Beo.

Ireland currently exports 90 per cent of domestically produced beef and dairy while importing over 80 per cent of the fruit and vegetables for sale on supermarket shelves.

“We have internalised the view that the reliable source of food is from long food chains,” says Fergal Anderson, founding member of Talamh Beo and a horticulture and woodland farmer in east Galway.

Janet Power, co-founder of Gorse Farm on the Carlow-Wexford border, believes there is an alternative to reliance on imported vegetables and fruit.

“It’s about creating viable farmer livelihoods, farmers who protect nature and provide healthy local food for communities. The basic income for small producers is about making these producers secure,” she says.

“There are no financial supports and no advisory services for small food producers in Ireland,” says Ruth Hegarty from Food Policy Ireland. And while Talamh Beo welcome the new Irish Horticulture Growers-Retailers charter, its focus is more on developing local food networks outside the large supermarket chains.

Talamh Beo also suggests public procurement of local food – alongside the basic income – would ensure financial viability. Many of these small food producers are selling directly to customers or to restaurants and local shops.

Dr Matthew O’Neill is the author of the paper Transforming Ireland’s Food System: Barriers and Opportunities, for the Institute of International and European Affairs.

He says income supports for local food producers would need to sit alongside “fair prices, access to land and reliable routes to market”.

“Supporting small producers could help sustain economic activity through local markets,” he says. “But I would be cautious about claiming a significant national food-security impact without evidence of how much additional production the scheme would support and who would be able to access it.

“Local food security is not just about growing more food nearby. It is also about whether people can afford that food and whether producers can earn a decent living supplying it.”

There are already some examples of farmers receiving a basic income as part of specific regional projects. Roger Ahern, who runs Green Man’s Garden, a small market garden in Co Cork, get a basic income of €1,400 a month from Bioregioning South East Ireland, a philanthropically funded organisation supporting agricultural innovation.

“It allows me plan for the long-term hire of someone to work with me so that I can run courses for children in growing vegetables,” says Ahern.

Jo Poulton, a vegetable grower from England is the founder of the Basic Income for Farmers in the UK. Three pilot basic income schemes are in train across the UK, including a Scotland-wide initiative promoting a basic income scheme for all farmers, farm workers and crofters.

The Grow More Growers basic income scheme includes four landowners in Buckinghamshire who rent land to new growers, who are paid £1,000 a month (€1,184) for three years to establish new market gardens.

The rising cost of urban living is encouraging some young people to consider settling in the countryside if they can make a living from the land.

“You can make a living from a small amount of land,” says Janet Power who, with her partner, Jenny Watkins supplies restaurants from Gorse Farm, their organic market garden of one hectare.

The Feeding Ourselves Local Food Symposium in Trinity College Dublin heard testimonies from these and other small holders – many passionate about environmental stewardship and revitalising rural communities.

“There is a revolutionary potential of food to bring our communities together – to bring growers on the edge of our cities together with activists in the cities,” says Barry Ferguson, who offers practical training for market gardeners in Northern Ireland.

Yet the average age of Irish farmers is 59, and succession is an issue for one in five farmers across Ireland.

Chris Smaje, an author and vegetable farmer in Somerset who spoke at the event, says local and global policies do not support small vegetable producers.

“Farmers are pressurised to produce what they can produce most advantageously and sell it on the global food market which results in too much of the wrong food in the wrong places going to the wrong people,” he says.

The author of books including A Small Farm Future, Smaje says reinventing small farms and local production is a key to solving climate change and resilience to geopolitical tensions.

“We need to get beyond the atomised global consumers meeting atomised global producers and instead have local communities of growers and producers where we meet and eat food,” he says.

He acknowledges developing such a local food economy would require new skill sets and an understanding of the limits of what can be produced locally.

But giving small-scale food producers the opportunity to thrive alongside the dominant grass-based livestock production for the export market could contribute to revitalised rural economies for the benefit of all.

]]><![CDATA[Ann Dunne, daughter of Dunnes Stores founder, dies]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/12/ann-dunne-daughter-of-dunnes-stores-founder-dies/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/12/ann-dunne-daughter-of-dunnes-stores-founder-dies/Thu, 12 Nov 2026 10:28:03 +0000Ann Dunne, daughter of Dunnes Stores founder Bernard Dunne, has died.

According to a notice on the RIP.ie website, she died on October 17th peacefully “surrounded by her loving family and friends”, including sister Margaret Heffernan (84), the current chief executive of Dunnes Stores.

In an accompanying statement, her family said they would like to thank “everyone who has taken care of Ann in her latter years”.

It added that a family funeral has already taken place.

The death of Ann Dunne means Heffernan is the last remaining child of the late Nora and Bernard Dunne.

Her death has come less than a year after the death of Heffernan’s husband Andrew, who previously worked as a consultant endocrinologist at the Blackrock Clinic.

Ann Dunne was predeceased by her siblings Frank, Elizabeth, Therese and Ben, the last of whom died in November 2019.

Ben Dunne, who died at the age of 74, played a pivotal role in the expansion of Dunnes Stores, which was set up by his father and grew into the largest retail chain in the country with about 100 stores and a turnover of close to £1 billion (about €1.2 billion) at the time of his departure.

He was ousted from the company, which led to his sister Margaret Heffernan taking over, and later built up a chain of well-known gyms.

Heffernan, who has led the supermarket and department store chain since the early 1990s, has been credited with transforming the business into an upmarket retailer during her time in charge.

Following a restructuring in 2018, the Dunnes Stores group has been controlled through an entity called Better Value Unlimited Company. Due to its unlimited status, the firm is not required to publish financial figures such as turnover and profits.

Better Value Unlimited Company is led by Heffernan and two other directors, her daughter Anne Heffernan and niece Sharon McMahon.

]]>Shawn Williams<![CDATA[Nvidia board weighs Huang’s future as shares tumble]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/12/nvidia-board-weighs-huangs-future-as-shares-tumble/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/12/nvidia-board-weighs-huangs-future-as-shares-tumble/Thu, 12 Nov 2026 07:59:37 +0000Nvidia is working with an outside firm to identify potential replacements for chief executive Jensen Huang.

In late US trading on Wednesday, Nvidia’s shares tumbled as much as 10 per cent following a report by The Wall Street Journal that Nvidia’s board was preparing to oust Huang from his role.

The board’s reported search for a replacement has come after details emerged of an affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy and a report alleging a separate affair with an employee.

The board was planning to meet as soon as Wednesday to determine his future, people familiar with the matter said.

Huang’s departure would bring down the curtain on an era during which he stoked the global artificial-intelligence boom and became a geopolitical star. It would leave one of the world’s most valuable companies in need of a new leader.

The company has tapped an outside firm to identify potential candidates following reports of multiple extramarital affairs by Huang.

For more than three decades, Huang’s has taken a hands-on role in shaping Nvidia’s strategy.

Beyond developing the AI accelerators that now dominate the artificial intelligence landscape, Huang has turned the company into an industry kingmaker that oversees a sprawling web of customers, suppliers, partners and investments.

The upheaval at the company, scheduled to report its quarterly results on November 17th, risks further shaking confidence in the AI trade that’s driven much of this year’s global equity rally before coming under increased scrutiny from investors over stretched valuations and the scale of spending on AI.

Wall Street sentiment toward Nvidia is starting to crack. Bernstein was the latest firm to downgrade the stock, cutting its rating to market perform from outperform while lowering its price target to $200 from $400. Baird earlier downgraded the shares to neutral, while Morgan Stanley removed them as a top pick.

The estimated fair value of Nvidia without Huang will fall by about 25 per cent to $225 per share versus an estimate of $300 per share if he stays as chief executive, according to Yorkville Ives, adding that the technology world and the board is quickly realising the situation is getting worse by the day as more news comes out.

Last week, tech stocks around the world plunged on worries that the Democrats’ sweep of Congress in the US midterms may lead to tougher oversight of the AI industry.

“Nvidia’s latest developments could weigh on sentiment across the broader AI trade, but we see selective opportunities emerging among semiconductor companies that can offer credible second source alternatives for critical AI chips,” said Gary Tan, a portfolio manager at Allspring Global Investments.

On Wednesday, US stocks rallied amid optimism over the AI trade as shares of CoreWeave surged 25 per cent on an upbeat outlook, OpenAI’s quarterly revenue reached $10 billion and Anthropic initial public offering was said to be multiple times oversubscribed. The Nasdaq 100 jumped 2.3 per cent while the S&P 500 climbed 1.3 per cent.

“Renewed AI optimism following CoreWeave’s stronger-than-expected earnings is being offset by the worsening management crisis at Nvidia,” said Tan Altundag, an investment manager for emerging equities at Pictet Asset Management. – Bloomberg

]]>Manuel Orbegozo

   <title>EU-Einigung auf breites Verhandlungsteam</title>
   <description>Die Staats- und Regierungschefs der EU haben sich darauf geeinigt, wer Europa bei künftigen Gesprächen über ein Ende des Ukraine-Krieges vertreten soll: Das „europäische Verhandlungsteam für den Frieden in der Ukraine“ werde „aus den Institutionen der Europäischen Union und den E5“ bestehen, sagte EU-Ratspräsident Antonio Costa am Freitag nach dem informellen EU-Gipfel in Dublin. Bei den E5-Ländern handelt es sich um Deutschland, Großbritannien, Frankreich, Italien und Polen.</description>

A new hub has opened at the University of Oxford to support research cooperation with Poland, offering grants for academic projects, visits, training and workshops.

The Oxford Poland Hub, which its organisers describe as Poland’s first initiative of its kind anywhere in the world, will also hold public events exploring Polish history, language and culture.

We’re proud to have worked on the Oxford-Poland Hub & helped make it a reality together with great partners 🇵🇱🇬🇧

Huge thanks to:
🔹 @UniofOxford & @JesusOxford, esp. Prof Paulina Kewes & Dr Marek Naczyk
🔹 Ministry of Science and Higher Education & Minister @MarcinKulasek 🧵 pic.twitter.com/LghfpOhptC

— Polish Embassy UK 🇵🇱 (@PolishEmbassyUK) November 12, 2026

“The launch of the Oxford-Poland Hub is an exciting new chapter in Oxford’s longstanding relationship with Poland,” said the University of Oxford’s vice-chancellor, Irene Tracey. “[It] will create new opportunities for academic exchange, collaborative research and partnership between Oxford and Poland.”

The centre is initially funded for three years by Poland’s National Agency for Academic Exchange (NAWA), with support from the science and higher education ministry. It will operate within The Oxford Research Centre in the Humanities (TORCH).

“The Oxford Poland Hub…gives us a permanent institutional presence at one of the world’s leading academic centres,” said Wojciech Karczewski, NAWA’s director general.

“We see it as an investment in long-term partnerships that will enable researchers from Poland and Oxford to tackle increasingly ambitious research challenges together.”

 

The University of Oxford is the oldest university in the English-speaking world and one of the most prestigious. It ranked first globally in the latest Times Higher Education World University Rankings.

The new centre will offer grants of up to £5,000 (26,400 zloty) to support research projects or academic visits and up to £10,000 for academic workshops. Training scholarships are due to be introduced from the hub’s second year.

All researchers affiliated with the University of Oxford will be eligible to apply for funding if their work involves collaboration with researchers based in Poland. The hub will focus on humanities and social sciences as well as cooperation with Oxford’s libraries and museums.

The hub will also organise public lectures, exhibitions and events related to Polish history, language and culture for the academic community and Oxford’s residents, including its Polish community.

🇵🇱🇬🇧 Oxford-Poland Hub oficjalnie otwarty! Polska nauka zyskuje nowe możliwości współpracy z Uniwersytetem Oksfordzkim.

W uroczystym otwarciu wziął udział minister nauki i szkolnictwa wyższego Marcin Kulasek. Centrum powstało dzięki współpracy Ministerstwa Nauki i Szkolnictwa… pic.twitter.com/bZaCdM3Y53

— Ministerstwo Nauki i Szkolnictwa Wyższego (@MNiSW_GOV__PL) November 10, 2026

The hub was inaugurated on Monday at Jesus College, one of Oxford University’s colleges, with Poland’s science and higher education minister, Marcin Kulasek, and Rafał Wiśniewski, chargé d’affaires at the Polish Embassy in London, among those attending.

“Poland and the United Kingdom have for many years developed strong cooperation in science and higher education through joint research projects, academic mobility programmes and institutional partnerships,” Kulasek said. “The Oxford–Poland Hub opens a new chapter in this cooperation.”

The centre is directed by Paulina Kewes, a professor of English literature at Oxford who was born in Poland. Professor Norman Davies, the renowned historian of Poland and an honorary fellow at St Antony’s College, Oxford, attended the launch.

The inaugural lecture, given by Dariusz Wójcik, a professor at the National University of Singapore and honorary research associate at the University of Oxford, discussed Maria Czaplicka, the renowned Polish academic who in 1916 became Oxford’s first female lecturer of anthropology.

A Belgian court has overturned an order to seize funds from Poland’s air-traffic control agency, PANSA, as part of pharmaceutical giant Pfizer’s efforts to enforce a €1.3 billion claim for COVID-19 vaccines Poland ordered but later refused to receive and pay for.

The ruling, issued on Thursday, followed a legal challenge by PANSA to the freezing of its funds. It argued that it was not a party to the dispute between Pfizer and the Polish state.

❗️Dziś Francuskojęzyczny Sąd Pierwszej Instancji w Brukseli wydał korzystny dla strony polskiej wyrok w sprawie zajęcia opłat trasowych należnych @PANSA_PL , pobieranych za pośrednictwem EUROCONTROL.

Sąd uznał zajęcie za bezzasadne i uchylił postanowienie, na podstawie którego… pic.twitter.com/EHvHZnL6ab

— Ministerstwo Zdrowia (@MZ_GOV_PL) November 12, 2026

In July this year, PANSA announced that it had been cut off from the fees paid to it by the European Organisation for the Safety of Air Navigation (Eurocontrol), which manages air traffic in Europe. Around 80% of PANSA’s revenue comes from those fees.

Eurocontrol is based in Belgium, which is where Pfizer has been fighting its legal battle against Poland over the unpaid vaccines. The move to freeze PANSA’s funds was part of Pfizer’s efforts to claim money it had been awarded from Poland by a Belgian court in April this year.

Prime Minister Donald Tusk pledged government support to ensure PANSA had sufficient funds to maintain its operations and assured that air safety would not be compromised.

Poland’s air-traffic control agency has been cut off from most of its revenue as part of efforts by pharmaceutical giant Pfizer to enforce a Belgian court ruling requiring Poland to pay €1.3bn for Covid vaccines it ordered but then refused to receive https://t.co/Nd9IyLqmmf

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 11, 2026

On Thursday this week, PANSA announced that its legal challenge to the seizure of its assets by bailiffs had been successful, though it noted that the ruling can still be appealed.

Poland’s health ministry, which has been involved in overseeing the legal battle with Pfizer, said that the Belgian court had confirmed that PANSA’s funds belong to the agency itself, not to the State treasury.

“The agency is a separate legal entity; it possesses its own assets and manages its own finances independently. It is not liable for the obligations of the State treasury; therefore, its funds cannot be used to satisfy Pfizer’s claims against Poland,” wrote the ministry.

 

In comments to Polish Radio, PANSA chief Magdalena Jaworska-Maćkowiak said the agency had become a hostage in a case “that did not, in fact, concern us”.

“It stemmed from an entirely separate dispute,” she noted. “This created extreme difficulties, as we were relying on a ‘bridge’ financing arrangement that, under current law, could not provide us with long-term stability.”

Pfizer, meanwhile, said Thursday’s court decision affected only one avenue of its efforts to enforce payment of the April ruling. “We are taking ​appropriate steps through ​established legal ⁠and contractual mechanisms to ensure compliance with the court’s [April] decision,” it added, quoted by Reuters.

Sąd w Brukseli uznał sprzeciw PAŻP wobec zajęcia komorniczego dokonanego na wniosek Pfizer za zasadny i uchylił postanowienie z 25 czerwca 2026 r., stanowiące podstawę zajęcia komorniczego. Rozstrzygnięcie jest zatem korzystne dla PAŻP, ale wyrok nie jest jeszcze prawomocny.

— PANSA (@PANSA_PL) November 12, 2026

The dispute stems from Poland’s refusal in 2022 to accept and pay for COVID-19 vaccine doses ordered from Pfizer under European Union procurement agreements.

In April 2022, the then health minister, Adam Niedzielski, invoked a force majeure clause following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022

Poland, which by then had already sold or donated some of its surplus vaccines, argued the mass influx of Ukrainian refugees strained its public finances, while its cases of Covid infections had dropped.

Romania later made a similar decision to not comply with the contract. In 2023, Pfizer sued both countries in Belgium, the country where the contracts were signed. Over the course of the case, Poland also argued that Pfizer had potentially abused its market position.

A Belgian court has ordered Poland to pay US pharmaceutical giant Pfizer around €1.3 billion for Covid vaccines ordered by the European Commission on behalf of member states during the pandemic but which the Polish government later refused to receive https://t.co/1ZtPgl8Y3o

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 2, 2026

But in April, a Belgian court rejected those arguments and ruled in Pfizer’s favour, ordering Poland to accept approximately 64 million vaccine doses and pay more than 5.6 billion zloty, plus interest and legal costs.

Poland appealed against the judgment in August 2026. The health ministry said on Thursday it would not disclose details of its legal arguments or planned procedural steps while the proceedings remain ongoing.

By Leo Greenberg

Speaking to Fox News in late October, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky admitted a widely known but uncomfortable truth: Ukraine needs its refugees back.

“We need 9.5 million people – who lost their homes, who are abroad, everywhere – we need them to come back to Ukraine…to rebuild their country,” he said.

Zelensky:

We need 9.5 million people who lost their housing, who are abroad everywhere — we need them to come back to Ukraine, just to live and to build their country. pic.twitter.com/Xu2Ld4eGOu

— Clash Report (@clashreport) October 21, 2026

Unfortunately for Ukraine, all signs point in the opposite direction: Ukrainians abroad are deferring or abandoning thoughts of return.

A large proportion of those refugees – almost one million of them – live in Poland, where Ukrainians, including migrants who arrived before 2022, have provided an economic and demographic boon. But their continued stay has also posed social and political challenges, as a country with no history of mass immigration grapples with the new reality of a sizable non-citizen minority.

This has left the refugees themselves in a state of limbo: torn between a homeland that wants them back, and to which many would like to return, but where conditions do not allow for it; and an adopted home where they have created new lives but where social tensions and logistical hurdles have meant persistent uncertainty.

A new reality sets in

When Solomiia Pischana, a Ukrainian woman in her late twenties, fled from Kyiv to Poland in the wake of Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, she hoped to go back that same year.

When Kyiv was secured by Ukrainian forces, a return seemed possible. In late 2022, Pischana started travelling back home to see family and friends. “I was really living between two countries. I thought a lot about going back.”

Yet quickly, a new reality set in on her visits: “In winter it became basically impossible to stay there – the constant explosions.” In Poland, by contrast, “everyone put the emphasis on helping me, on helping Ukrainians.”

In a photo essay, we look at the lives of three of the million or so Ukrainian refugees who remain in Poland one year on from Russia's invasion: Liudmyla, a mother; Vlad, an amputee soldier; and Viktoria, a high-school student https://t.co/kdOpEgt2LB

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 21, 2023

For many Ukrainians, Pischana’s story will feel familiar. When Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Poland became the main waystation for Ukrainians on their way out. Millions crossed the border, and while many went on to other destinations in Europe and beyond, initially more than one million remained in Poland.

The Polish state reacted quickly, assigning more than a million special identification numbers for Ukrainian refugees – known as “PESEL-UKR” – and enrolling them in the same housing and benefits systems used by Polish citizens.

So too did Polish society, with a majority of Poles working in some way to assist Ukraine or arriving refugees, and many hosting refugees in their homes.

Around 77% of Poles have been involved in helping refugees from Ukraine, for which purpose they spent around €2 billion out of their own pockets, a new study by @PIE_NET_PL has found https://t.co/xWu8JWNMui

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 28, 2022

For Ukraine, the exodus of around six million refugees meant a raft of problems. Some 650,000 military-age men left the country, while schools had to figure out how to provide remote instruction for two million children abroad.

Most of all, the refugee crisis worsened Ukraine’s demographic challenges. Before 2022, Ukraine’s population of 42 million had already been shrinking and ageing. Now, Ukraine’s minister for social policy estimates that just 22-25 million people remain in Ukrainian-controlled territory. Two thirds of Ukrainian businesses are short of workers.

Initially, many hoped for a brief war. But, as the reality of a long, grinding conflict dawned, it became clear that Ukraine could no longer plan for an imminent influx of able-bodied adults: surveys by Kyiv’s Centre for Economic Strategies show that the proportion of refugees intending to return dropped from 74% in November 2022 to 43% in January 2026.

“Rather chaotic” attempts to connect with refugees

This reality has meant that, while Ukraine needs its people back, it also knows that it cannot compel people to return to a life defined by rolling blackouts and the ever-present threat of drones and ballistic missiles.

As a result, Ukraine’s efforts to encourage and support refugee return have been haphazard and limited.

Ukraine has one deputy minister, Ilona Havronska, who is armed with just 150 million hryvnia (13.1 million zloty, €3 million) in this year’s state budget to maintain connections with refugees abroad and support their return.

Havronska has sought to create a network of “Unity Hubs,” paid for by foreign governments, where Ukrainian refugees can confer with trained consultants about returning home. Such facilities have opened in Stockholm, Prague and Berlin, with the latter receiving 5,000 visits since opening in May.

⚡️Ukraine, Germany agree to open 'Unity Hub' for Ukrainian refugees in Berlin.

"This is a professional space that brings together community, business, and cultural initiatives," National Unity Minister Oleksii Chernyshov said.https://t.co/rlTq3MpOd0

— The Kyiv Independent (@KyivIndependent) February 15, 2025

So far, however, no hub has opened in Poland, whose interior ministry told Notes from Poland: “To be frank, the Ukrainian side, Minister Havronska, they haven’t approached us much about this recently.”

Ukraine’s other major effort, a digital platform called “Dodomu” (“Homeward”), allows users to make a return plan and check off items on a digital to-do list, such as transferring medical files, verifying IDs, and registering children in Ukrainian schools.

Since launching in June, Dodomu has been used by 4,500 people in Poland, of whom 600 have completed a questionnaire about their possibility of return.

Ukraine’s efforts to reach out to refugees abroad have been “rather chaotic”, according to Olena Babakova, a Polish-Ukrainian journalist and researcher who studies migration.

 

However, a survey by the UNHCR suggests that it may not make much difference: Ukrainian refugees ranked “support for return” as less important to their decision-making than security, economic opportunities, and housing in Ukraine. Nevertheless, for older refugees and those from now-occupied territories in eastern Ukraine, large numbers cited additional information as one of their key needs.

Valentina Bryl, a Ukrainian who has lived in Poland since before 2022 and is now an HR specialist in Wrocław, notes that returning to Ukraine would mean she would have to “start everything from the beginning – my job, my life. It’s not just about safety.”

So while Bryl says that she visits Ukraine often – taking the 25-hour rail journey from Wrocław to Kharkiv to see her husband, who is serving at the front – she hasn’t made use of Dodomu or thought about the Unity Hubs. She has no intention of moving back.

From welcome to wariness in Poland

Yet for the million or so Ukrainian refugees in Poland, as well as the hundreds of thousands of Ukrainian economic migrants who came before 2022, a growing consideration is not only the conditions in Ukraine, but also the environment they face in their adopted homeland.

Poland welcomed refugees in 2022 and has supported them since. It has also benefited economically from their presence, with Ukrainian refugees estimated to have raised national GDP by 2.4% in 2025.

Ukrainian refugees boosted Poland’s GDP by 2.4% in 2025, the equivalent of €21.5bn, according to a report by the UN @Refugees agency and @Deloitte

At the same time, their growing presence in the labour market had no negative impact on employment or wages https://t.co/lcsuIwBzpy

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 8, 2026

However, there have been growing social and political tensions. During the 2025 presidential election, even liberal candidates proposed restricting child benefits for Ukrainian refugees.

The eventual winner, right-wing candidate Karol Nawrocki, in one of his first acts as president, vetoed an extension of Ukrainians’ temporary protections, before signing a revised extension that restricted benefits.

Those political changes reflect shifting attitudes in society. A June 2026 report from the Institute of Political Critique (IKP) described last year’s election campaign as a “Rubicon”, citing testimony from Ukrainian refugees that the public environment had become more hostile and historical issues had surfaced.

Pischana told Notes from Poland that, while she is “surrounded by good people” in Poland, she has noticed that “old topics like the Volhynia massacre are coming up much more”, referring to the mass slaughter of Poles by Ukrainian nationalists in World War Two. “Just walking down the street and speaking Ukrainian, it’s started to feel a bit more dangerous,” she added.

Police data show that the number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland was 30% higher in the first half of this year than in the same period of 2025.

The number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland is up 30% so far this year, police data show.

The figures come following recent high-profile cases of verbal and physical attacks against Ukrainians, who are Poland's largest immigrant group https://t.co/pcTsJddDz7

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 17, 2026

Myroslava Keryk, who leads Ukraiński Dom, a hub that provides services to Ukrainian refugees in Warsaw, told Notes from Poland that her staff have faced growing harassment.

She described a slew of AI-generated videos depicting them demanding Poles pay greater taxes to support refugees, as well as sexualised, fake accounts made of her employees on online apps.

Poland’s government has condemned the recent spate of hate crimes and accused the opposition and Nawrocki of stirring up such social vitriol. Meanwhile, it has begun preparing for Ukrainian refugees’ longer-term stay.

Ukrainian refugees’ current PESEL-UKR status is tied to the EU’s temporary protections, now set to expire in March 2028. So this year, the government introduced a new “CUKR” status, valid for three years of residence after it is granted. Some 75,000 Ukrainians have already submitted applications.

President Nawrocki has signed into law a government bill ending the special status granted in 2022 to Ukrainian refugees, who will now be treated on the same legal basis as other foreigners.

Nawrocki said he is "ending the era of unconditional privileges" https://t.co/BzY7wrdl49

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 20, 2026

This new status, however, is only a step on the path to long-term stability. CUKR, unlike most refugees’ current “UKR” status, counts toward the five years of legal stay required to apply for long-term EU resident status. However, its three-year duration means holders need to secure two additional years of legal protection in Poland before applying for long-term residency.

Polish state policies have not always made things easy for refugees. New restrictions on benefits and on travel outside of Poland have made refugees careful. Despite that, many appreciated the legal and logistical clarity of Poland’s approach, typified by the new CUKR status.

Refugees’ primary fears have concerned their social environment, not their legal status. Babakova put it neatly: “Ukrainians in Poland feel very connected to Ukrainian society, but not the state. At the same time, they have come to trust the Polish state, but not Polish society.”

The citizenship question

At the same time, a growing number of Ukrainians are thinking of obtaining citizenship, which would allow them to travel more freely and vote in Polish elections.

An August survey of Ukrainian refugees in Poland found that a plurality (35%) listed obtaining citizenship as the “most desired form of assistance” to make their lives easier.

In 2025, a record 19,000 foreigners, more than half of whom (10,000) were Ukrainian, were granted citizenship in Poland.

Poland granted citizenship to a record 19,135 foreigners in 2025, up 17% from the previous year and almost five times higher than a decade ago.

Over half of recipients were Ukrainians, followed by Belarusians, Russians, Vietnamese and Turks https://t.co/FoyWd5UPJx

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 15, 2026

But since then, Poland has moved to restrict access to citizenship – to make it “an earned privilege, not a formal certificate”, in the words of the interior ministry.

The plans include extending the required period of legal residence from five to eight years, requiring a loyalty declaration, mandating advanced knowledge of Polish, and introducing an exam on Polish history and values.

Pischana wants to become a Polish citizen: “I’ve thought that it would be logical […] I’ve lived for years in Poland. I know the language.” She added that her university thesis focuses on Polish history: she’s writing a comparison of Ukrainian and Polish songs with political or social themes, from the 1980s to the present day.

Kamil Kisiel, deputy director for the department of internal affairs and migration at Poland’s interior ministry, told Notes from Poland that the new citizenship laws, soon to be announced, will be tough: “For now, being more restrictive is the way to go, so that we can manage people’s expectations”.

The proportion of Poles who hold a negative view of relations with Ukraine has risen to the highest level ever recorded by state research agency CBOS

Meanwhile, the proportion who believe reconciliation with Ukraine is possible is at its lowest ever level https://t.co/YYBCFkVxNr

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 12, 2026

Kisiel was also up front that the Polish government does not envision many Ukrainians in Poland becoming citizens. No more than a few tens of thousands of Ukrainians have obtained Polish citizenship in the past decade, and those who arrived in 2022 are not yet eligible to apply.

Instead, Kisiel highlighted, “long-term EU residence is…the sort of stability people should expect”.

Karina, a Ukrainian woman who has been in Poland since she was 15 and did not want her surname published, says that she wants Polish citizenship as it offers “a chance to travel around the European Union, go to Spain. You can also go to America, because a Polish passport gives you visa-free travel; unfortunately, with a Ukrainian one you can’t.”

Head in Poland, heart in Ukraine

Barring a major change in the course of the war, Ukraine may even become one of the countries, including Ireland and Armenia, whose diasporas are as large or larger than their domestic population – a scenario that Havronska, the Ukrainian deputy minister, told Notes from Poland she is planning for.

At the same time, social tensions and citizenship restrictions in Poland reflect the fact that refugees are challenging Poland’s identity: since the eradication and movement of Jews, Ukrainians and Germans during and after World War Two, Poland has been a largely monoethnic nation, accustomed to one language, one faith, and one national identity. The approximately 1.5 million Ukrainians in Poland have changed that.

For Pischana, her head is in Poland while her heart remains in Ukraine, saying that she feels more attached to the culture of her homeland. “It’s a pity I can’t develop in my own country, because there’s room to do it there,” she says.

For Bryl, it’s been harder to keep close to Ukraine: “I have work, I have other responsibilities…You no longer want to read, you don’t want to get angry at some bad news”.

At the beginning, she said, she felt she had a fully Ukrainian life – just one that was put on pause. But, she adds, “when it’s already been going on for five years, and it’s still unknown how long it’ll go on, well, it’s hard to keep it on pause.”

By Aleks Szczerbiak

Poland’s escalating Constitutional Tribunal (TK) dispute is no longer simply a legal argument about contested appointments but a struggle over who defines constitutional legitimacy.

As the liberal-centrist government and right-wing opposition and president advance rival rule-of-law claims, the conflict risks entrenching a system of legal dualism in which judicial authority depends on political allegiance rather than broad constitutional consent.

The roots of the crisis

Poland’s 15-member TK is a powerful body that rules on the constitutionality of the country’s laws. The roots of the current dispute trace back to late 2015 and began immediately prior to the right-wing Law and Justice (PiS) party taking office following its October parliamentary election victory.

In its final weeks in power, the outgoing government, led by the liberal-centrist Civic Platform (PO, now Civic Coalition: KO), fast-tracked the appointment of five tribunal members who were replacing those whose terms were set to expire in November and December.

Upon winning an outright parliamentary majority, the incoming PiS-led government refused to recognise these appointments, elected a slate of five new tribunal members, and party-backed President Andrzej Duda swore them in.

Fifteen months since the change of government, Poland's rule-of-law crisis continues – indeed, many Poles think the situation has got worse.@J_Jaraczewski explains the roots of the crisis, what its impact has been, and how it might be resolved https://t.co/7KOCURV3dU

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 17, 2025

The tribunal (still largely composed of pre-2015 judges) ruled that three of the outgoing parliament’s appointments were lawful, so only two of the new ones could stand. PiS refused to accept this, creating the so-called “understudy” judges (dublerzy) controversy.

As further vacancies arose, the new parliament gradually installed its nominees, culminating in the appointment at the end of 2016 of one of them, Julia Przyłębska, as tribunal president. Przyłębska’s leadership was contested on procedural grounds, as was that of her 2024 successor Bogdan Święczkowski, a former senior prosecutor closely aligned with the 2015-23 PiS administration.

All of this led to the then-opposition parties and much of the Polish legal and the EU political establishments denouncing the tribunal as legally compromised and politically captured.

Total non-cooperation

Following the autumn 2023 parliamentary election, a new coalition government headed up by KO leader Donald Tusk embraced a policy of total non-cooperation with the tribunal, refusing to publish its rulings.

The battle for control took a new turn when, after initially not filling any tribunal vacancies, from March 2026 onwards the new parliament elected successive waves of new members, reaching eight by September.

However, PiS-aligned President Karol Nawrocki (who succeeded Duda in August 2025) refused to swear in five of these nominees, including former minister and close Tusk ally Maciej Berek. In response, the government took the unprecedented step of swearing in the contested nominees directly in parliament, a move that both Nawrocki and Święczkowski rejected as illegal.

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 14, 2026

The conflict escalated sharply at the end of last month, when, backed by the government and tribunal members elected by the current parliamentary majority, Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, one of the five contested nominees but having the longest judicial tenure, asserted her seniority to order a one-month suspension of Święczkowski and his deputy Bartłomiej Sochański in their official duties and assumed temporary control.

Justice minister Waldemar Żurek submitted requests to lift Święczkowski and Sochański’s immunity as the newly appointed members, and the new nominees entered the tribunal building under State Protection Service (UOP) escort.

This triggered protests by right-wing opposition supporters at the building’s gates, prompting a heavy police presence and tense stand-off. The severity of this was underscored when Nawrocki cut short an official visit to Senegal mid-flight, returned to Warsaw and entered the tribunal building in the early hours, condemning what he described as a violation of the constitutional order.

During a visit to the Constitutional Tribunal last night, President Nawrocki clashed physically and verbally with judges involved in an attempt to take control of the court.

Korwin-Piotrowska then convened a tribunal general assembly which critics argued lacked the legally required two-thirds quorum because only eight of its 15 nominal members (the newly elected ones, including the five who had not taken the presidential oath) attended.

Her supporters maintained that the quorum was met because the suspension of Święczkowski and Sochański, and exclusion of the last remaining “understudy” judge, reduced the pool of eligible members to 12.

The government’s “transitional justice” logic

For the Tusk government and its legal defenders, these exceptional executive and parliamentary countermeasures were framed through the logic of “transitional justice”: as painful and extraordinary but necessary to restore the rule of law after PiS had violated the constitution and European standards, systematically packing the tribunal with political loyalists.

Justifying its non-recognition of tribunal rulings, the government argued that the presence of three defectively elected “understudy” members and their successors, together with Przyłębska’s and Święczkowski’s procedurally flawed presidential appointments, fundamentally “contaminated” the entire body, thereby invalidating its rulings.
