But he says this is because of the legal chaos deliberately created by the former PiS government https://t.co/AWlM6hRLie

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 11, 2024

To provide what it argued was authoritative external confirmation of this defect, the government relied heavily on landmark European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) and EU Court of Justice (CJEU) rulings which determined that, thus constituted, the tribunal could no longer be considered a legitimate body established by legal standards.

From this perspective, refusing to recognise the tribunal’s allegedly unlawful rulings was framed as the only available mechanism to neutralise a partisan weapon that PiS had left behind to block the government’s legislative agenda.

Alternative parliamentary swearing-in procedures were justified on the grounds that the president’s role in receiving oaths was purely ceremonial, not a constitutionally mandated requirement.

 

Despite his recent political role, Berek’s appointment was defended on the basis that he played more of a technocratic-expert role within the government, and was highly qualified to undertake the extraordinary transitional measures required to repair a damaged institution.

Defenders of the tribunal leadership’s suspension and occupation of its headquarters argued that by blocking the new nominees from taking up their roles, Święczkowski had paralysed the institution and decisive measures were necessary to restore its proper functioning.

A “coup d’état”?

PiS and Nawrocki, on the other hand, maintained that the Tusk government’s actions amounted to an authoritarian attempt to operate completely outside of constitutional powers, treating legality as an option when it conflicted with its political agenda.

They insisted that all of its 2015 appointments were in full accordance with the law, correcting an improper attempt by the outgoing PO-dominated parliament to entrench its influence after electoral defeat, and that the tribunal’s ruling on the legality of these three “understudy” judges went beyond its jurisdiction.

Successive tribunal general assemblies, they argued, validly and legally selected Przyłębska and then Święczkowski as presidents, and the Tusk government had no constitutional right to pick and choose which tribunal rulings it would recognise. They said that, by delaying the election of some new members when vacancies arose, the government violated existing procedures.

The constitution, they said, explicitly required these new nominees to take their oaths directly “before the president” and that by conducting improper parliamentary swearing-in ceremonies they had effectively renounced their offices.

The International Commission of Jurists has criticised the takeover of Poland’s constitutional court, saying it “contravenes international standards on the independence of the judiciary”

But it also criticised the president for refusing to swear in judges https://t.co/2kBv3GT20d

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 4, 2026

The candidacy of Berek, a recently active politician with doubtful professional qualifications, they said represented its own form of institutional capture and selective legality.

The suspension of the tribunal leadership and occupation of its headquarters amounted to an unlawful power grab or “coup d’état” that completely disregarded established constitutional procedures.

PiS rejected the “contamination” thesis and argued vigorously that Poland had never transferred jurisdiction over the organisation of the national judiciary to EU institutions and European courts, who had no authority to evaluate the legality of tribunal appointments.

They accused the EU political establishment of double standards, weaponising “rule-of-law” arguments to help a politically aligned government while ignoring the Tusk administration’s own executive overreach.

PiS also argued that by delegitimising a tribunal which had in the past ruled that the Polish Constitution superseded EU law, the Tusk government was paving the way for controversial social and economic policies to be pushed through without any domestic judicial oversight.

Tusk’s liberal critics

On the other hand, more ideologically supportive liberal critics of the Tusk government’s approach acknowledged the original 2015 irregularities but warned that selective non-recognition of an entire institution, combined with attempts to install a new tribunal without presidential participation, risked creating the same dual legitimacy problem that they accused PiS of having started.

They stressed that lasting repair required broad political consensus and careful adherence to formal procedures so that future majorities did not simply invert the non-recognition tactic. They noted the tension with earlier condemnations of PiS for elevating politically aligned figures or recently active politicians.

While sympathetic to the goal of reforming what they believed was a deeply compromised tribunal, these critics argued that, by employing legally questionable shortcuts and executive force, the Tusk government risked setting dangerous precedents and deepening the very disorder that it was claiming to correct.

Interestingly, the government’s broader “transitional justice” justificatory logic – that ordinary procedures would not adequately address a systemic capture and the priority had to be functional restoration rather than abstract purity – mirrored the arguments PiS itself advanced for its own judicial reforms after 2015.

The right-wing party argued that the post-1989 judiciary remained dominated by a post-communist elite that required deep structural overhaul rather than incremental change.

A high-risk escalation

The latest escalation is likely to entrench and intensify the profound systemic polarisation that characterises the Polish political scene, for a long-time embodied in the KO-PiS duopoly, with the conflict framed in existential terms of either “restoring the rule of law” or “defending the constitutional order”.

This fierce dispute lies at the heart of the Tusk government’s broader political “reckoning” (rozliczenie) agenda involving visibly removing PiS’s influence from key institutions.

For the ruling coalition, this was a central 2023 election campaign message, and being seen to deliver on it is an absolute political necessity to satisfy and mobilise its electoral base. A confrontational approach thus serves to consolidate the government’s support among these core voters, who have grown increasingly impatient and want to see decisive action.

However, the government’s strategy is fraught with political risk. High-stakes tactics risk uniting its right-wing opponents and alienating moderate voters increasingly exhausted by endless, hyper-partisan institutional confrontation, legal brinkmanship and the optics of police deployments around a key state body.

They provide the president and right-wing opposition with a powerful counternarrative of constitutional vandalism ahead of the next parliamentary election.

Escalation is also straining relations within the ruling coalition, especially among more conservative or legalistic coalition partners who believe that a more fundamental constitutional “reset” based on a cross-party settlement is required to break the impasse in the longer term.

The leader of one of the parties in Poland’s ruling coalition has proposed a “constitutional reset” to resolve the crisis around the country’s top court.

It would involve removing all current judges and choosing new ones in a more consensual process https://t.co/xDwpRUVHxG

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 6, 2026

Internationally, although the EU political establishment remains supportive of the Tusk government’s actions, they invite uneasy scrutiny of the stability of Poland’s legal system and have drawn explicit criticism from the US embassy.

The reliance on a “transitional justice” framing that echoes PiS’s earlier justifications for systemic change, combined with the appointment to the tribunal of a recent minister despite prior criticisms of politicised nominations, also undercuts government claims of consistent principle and provides the right with a powerful narrative of hypocrisy.

Legal dualism

Ultimately, this bitter dispute has paved the way for a protracted and deeply destabilising “legal dualism” that could plague the Polish state for years to come, with a tribunal simultaneously legitimate and illegitimate depending on who holds power.

By treating the tribunal as an illegitimate entity when its nominees did not control it, the current government has established a precedent.

Even if it now appears to have secured a clear majority for its own nominees, a future right-wing government and sympathetic president will have every incentive to use the exact same playbook: treating the reconstituted tribunal as a captured instrument of the liberal establishment, and regarding it as no more legitimate than the Tusk government did the PiS-era one.

Consequently, the tribunal’s authority, and legal certainty in Poland more generally, have been further eroded, leaving the country without a widely accepted arbiter to resolve constitutional disputes. There are no immediate prospects for a durable resolution of this conflict.

Thousands of soldiers from 11 countries began military exercises in Poland today. They are the first organised by the so-called Coalition of the Willing, with the aim of preparing for a role in supporting Ukraine following a potential future peace deal with Russia.

The manoeuvres, which are being jointly led by France and the UK, are taking place in Nowa Dęba, around 100 kilometres from the Ukrainian border, and will last until 22 November.

The development has been condemned by Russia, which says it shows that Western countries are ignoring Moscow’s “legitimate security concerns” and “fueling the spiral of escalation”.​

🇫🇷🇬🇧 KOALICJA: The MNF-U is training to ensure a solid and lasting peace in Ukraine

The Multinational Force-Ukraine (MNF-U), formed from the Coalition of the Willing and under 🇫🇷🇬🇧command, is launching its first major exercise: KOALICJA

📅 November 9–22, 2026
📍In Poland,… pic.twitter.com/Ikcl1uY8N2

— The 🇫🇷 Joint Staff – Military operations (@FrenchForces) November 7, 2026

The plans were first announced in July by Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk following a summit of the Coalition of the Willing in Paris. The exercises, taking place on land, in the air, and at sea, are being conducted by the Multinational Force Ukraine (MNF-U), which serves as the military component of the coalition.

“This exercise will show that the Multinational Force-Ukraine is a real, capable, readily deployable force that represents a serious commitment from Coalition of the Willing nations to Ukraine’s long-term stability and security,” said Tom Bateman, the British lieutenant-general commanding MNF-U.

The British Ministry of Defence says that the exercise, which has been named “Koalicja” (meaning “Coalition” in Polish), “will test Allies’ readiness to support Ukraine and rebuild their Armed Forces once the conflict ends”.

France’s armed forces ministry, meanwhile, says that the aim is to ensure that MNF-U is “ready to deploy at the request of the Ukrainian government” in order to help “guarantee a robust and lasting peace in Ukraine”.

 

Around 2,800 troops are being deployed for the manoeuvres, with AFP reporting that this includes 1,100 from France alone. The British defence ministry says it has sent 300 personnel, as well as Typhoon and Voyager aircraft.

In addition, just under 2,000 Polish troops will take part, bringing the total to almost 5,000 personnel, reports Polska Zbrojna, a publication linked to the Polish defence ministry. Other countries taking part are Belgium, Estonia, Germany, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Spain, Sweden and Turkey.

Poland’s defence ministry says the exercises will “demonstrate how quickly participating nations can mobilise and establish forces capable of supporting Ukraine after the end of the war”.

However, although Poland is hosting the manoeuvres, the defence ministry reiterated the country’s position that “it would not send its own soldiers to Ukrainian territory” as part of any postwar settlement. Poland has made clear it intends instead to help provide logistical support.

France says that the deployment of forces to Ukraine would include sending instructors to help the country rebuild and strengthen its armed forces, while air missions would enable civlian aircraft to resume flying in Ukrainian airspace.

At sea, MNF-U forces could help clear mines from shipping routes in the Black Sea. The maritime component of the current exercises is being led by Turkey through a simulated operational exercise, without deploying troops to Poland itself.

France, the UK and Poland have emphasised, however, that the MNF-U forces would only be deployed once fighting in Ukraine has ceased and would not carry out peacekeeping or ceasefire-monitoring duties.

On Saturday, the spokeswoman for Russia’s foreign ministry, Maria Zakharova, condemned the exercises, saying that they make “absolutely clear that the West remains unwilling to take Russia’s legitimate security concerns into account and continues to fuel the spiral of escalation”.

She described the deployment of any foreign armed forces to Ukraine as “absolutely unacceptable” and said they would “create additional threats to Russia’s security”.

“Any military units in Ukraine will be regarded by the Russian armed forces as legitimate targets, with all the risks and consequences that entails,” warned Zakharova.

The exercises come as Ukraine and Russia meet the United States and others for peace talks in Abu Dhabi this week. Ukraine has repeatedly insisted that European security guarantees would be necessary for any peace agreement.

British defence secretary Wes Streeting suggested the exercises forecast precisely such a scenario: “This isn’t a hypothetical plan, it’s a real force, ready to help Ukraine once the fighting stops.”

Zakharova, however, says that the exercises are “yet another confirmation that the Europeans have no place at the negotiating table”.

Prepping young people for work is no good unless the government lowers the cost of employment to create more jobs, writes Helen Dickinson ahead of the release of the Alan Milburn’s NEET report

There is little point making young people work-ready if there are no jobs waiting for them. This is why government must address the rising costs and regulation that make entry-level jobs harder to create.

Picture a single decker bus. Forty young people, aged 16 to 24. The bus stops by the school and university; 23 get out to study. Next, it pulls up in the business district; another 12 get out for work. That leaves five young people not in education, employment or training (NEET).

This bus represents a whole generation of young people. The five people still on the bus represent nearly 1m young people who are NEET and cost the economy an eye-watering £125bn a year. A figure currently expected to rise.

But it’s more than the money. These young people miss out on the purpose and recognition that comes with a job, as well as opportunities to develop skills, build confidence and gain independence. Without experience, they struggle to find work; without work, they cannot gain experience. It’s a doom loop that risks leaving hundreds of thousands of young people behind.

Milburn report should focus on stimulating job creation

One in every eight young people is neither learning nor earning, failed by the system. They might be your child, your neighbour, your friend. We have a moral and economic duty to act.

This is what Alan Milburn’s upcoming report into Young People and Work, expected to be published next week, will set out to do. What he says, and how the government responds and acts, will determine whether this moral and economic imperative will be addressed.

Milburn will call on government to do more to prepare young people for the world of work. We need a benefits system that incentivises work. This might be helping people into part-time roles or changing the balance between in-work and out-of-work support. Doing so should reduce pressure on the welfare system and strengthen public finances.

But unless government also stimulates job creation, it simply won’t be enough. We need more jobs, including entry-level roles for those without experience or qualifications.

Retail is a vital source of these. Its 2.8m jobs offer flexible, local opportunities that don’t require qualifications. But between 2024 and 2027, retail’s employment costs will have risen by around £8.5bn. Over the same period, retail has lost over 120,000 roles. That’s a lot of full buses of young people with no job to head to.

Red tape is stifling employers

Economic growth has slowed to a crawl. The cost of employing young people has skyrocketed, so retailers have scaled back recruitment. When jobs are scarce, employers are choosy, leaving inexperienced young people at the back of the queue.

Government has two levers to boost job creation. First, put more money in people’s pockets, boosting spending power and giving employers a reason to hire. Secondly, cut the cost and risks of employing people. They must start to reverse the devastating employer National Insurance rises which have made entry-level jobs unaffordable for too many retailers. And they must ensure the implementation of new employment rights legislation avoids the adverse impacts on part-time and flexible work, so often relied upon by young people entering the workforce.

Retailers are taking action. Through Opening Shift, a BRC-DWP work experience initiative, over 50 retailers have pledged 11,000 placements, with the ambition of helping 100,000 young people into jobs. By giving young people the experience they need to get their foot on the career ladder, we can help break the cycle of unemployment. But only if these are new jobs. Simply moving the problem from one group of people to another won’t solve anything.

All eyes are now on the forthcoming Milburn report. Its recommendations must provide a turning point. But making young people work-ready is not enough. We must lower the costs of employment for businesses, and build a welfare system that rewards hard work. What the government does next will determine whether we get this generation moving or leave another million young people stuck on the bus.

Helen Dickinson is chief executive at the British Retail Consortium

Feldspar, a British sports tech company which says its smart athletics track can transform the Olympics within a decade, is in talks to raise up to £6m from new investors.

The firm’s team includes ex-GB sprinter Darren Campbell, senior figures from the Premier League and London Marathon, and former executives from SailGP and Formula E.

Feldspar’s founders believe its sensor plate technology can revolutionise sport by providing data to improve athlete performance and prevent injury but also enhance the spectacle.

“We’ve seen a lot of innovations in running shoes and training methods and so on but I haven’t seen anything that changes the surface itself,” founder Alvina Chen tells City AM.

“We are trying to bring in new products to not just optimise performance for the athletes and coaches, but to bring in a lot more fans and digitalise as well.”

Feldspar’s two products are a super-fast track layer that allows athletes to race or train harder, and the cloud-connected sensor-plate technology that can be installed beneath it.

The latter is, the company says, “the world’s first modular platform for continuous, real-time force measurement across sports surfaces”, and could facilitate recurring subscription revenues.

The smart track – created by the Cambridge Design Collective – collects data on horizontal, vertical and lateral force as well as centre pressure, delivering real-time insights that can be applied to training or turned into sophisticated content. 

Feldspar seeking strategic investors in seed round

Some 60m of track and 156 sensor plates were recently laid at the National Indoor Athletics Centre in Cardiff, where an 18-month pilot programme is now in progress.   

“What we’re doing here is potentially very transformational,” says executive director Tim Godfrey, formerly of SailGP, Formula E and triathlon’s PTO. “Because the underlying surface in which sports are played on is, in our mind, going to change forever if we get a lot of things right.”

He adds: “Nobody has been able to solve this particular problem of getting this level of biomechanical force data at scale. People do it already, but in a single force plate. No one’s done it to the scale we’ve done before. That’s the technological innovation.”

Feldspar’s first three years have been funded this far by the family of athlete-turned-entrepreneur Chen but the company is now in talks with investors over a seed round.

It is aiming to raise £5.5m to £6m, Chen says, and is keen to attract backing from sports organisations which may be able to play a role in the products’ evolution.

Godfrey adds: “We think it’s going to be strategic partners who understand, first and foremost, the value of the technology in a sporting environment. 

“We do have lots of interest from institutional investors as well, but they are going to possibly come a little bit further down the line, maybe Series A, Series B.”

Smart track tech at the Olympics and new Man Utd stadium?

While the sensor technology has been designed for running tracks, it could have a much wider application and provide insights for athletes, coaches and viewers in many sports.

Godfrey says court-based sports have already shown interest, and believes there is no reason why it shouldn’t be possible to extend it to cover the entirety of a full-size football pitch. 

“So you could imagine the new Manchester United football stadium that’s being built, our sensors all being connected underneath that,” says Godfrey. “Now, that’s quite blue sky thinking, but it’s 100 per cent achievable.”

Cost is currently a barrier to kitting out a whole athletics track with Feldspar’s sensor plates but that – and adoption in the Olympic Games – are among the company’s goals. 

“If a whole stadium wanted eight lanes, 400m with the sensors, today the price is not something that we would look to do, because we need to do a lot more development and get the manufacturing and the production and the supply chain,” says Godfrey. 

“But by 2036, we would make it achievable for a stadium or an event owner to purchase that.”

Chelsea FC have opened a pop-up store in Covent Garden in a bid to capitalise on Christmas shopping and festive tourist footfall.

The shop on Monmouth Street stocks club merchandise, including replica kits, Christmas jumpers and gifts and will be open seven days a week until 21 December.

It makes Chelsea the third football club with a retail outlet in central London, after Premier League rivals Liverpool and European champions Paris Saint-Germain.

“There is nowhere quite like Covent Garden during the Christmas season, which makes it the perfect home for Chelsea’s festive pop-up,” said the club’s lifestyle director Alexandra Currie. 

“We want supporters and shoppers alike to enjoy a little Chelsea magic this season, whether that means the latest kit, a gift for the Blues fan in the family or a piece from our festive collection.”

It follows the launch of the club’s festive range, That’s Proper Chels, which includes Christmas jumpers and pyjamas based on popular retro kit designs.

A percentage of sales will go to tackling loneliness in London through partnerships between the Chelsea Foundation and charities including Age UK Kensington & Chelsea, Katherine Low Settlement and Fulham Good Neighbours.

Football clubs in high streets across the world

Paris Saint-Germain led the way in establishing a bricks-and-mortar retail presence in central London when they opened a store on Oxford Street in 2023. 

Liverpool followed suit in May this year when they opened a club shop, also on Oxford Street, becoming the first Premier League club to do so.

PSG have club shops in 10 cities around the world, including New York City, Miami, Tokyo and Doha, while Liverpool boast more than 20 outlets from Chester and Dublin to Kuala Lumpur and Cape Town. 

Arsenal and Manchester City both have retail presence in New York, with the latter also in Abu Dhabi, home of their ownership.

Real Madrid have three stores in Barcelona – home of their fierce rivals, who have shops in the capital – as well as sites in Dubai, Mexico City and Bogota.

]]> 2477853Frank Dalleres Frank Dalleres Nvidia shares slip again as Wall Street weighs chip giant’s future https://www.cityam.com/nvidia-shares-slip-again-as-wall-street-weighs-chip-giants-future/ Fri, 13 Nov 2026 15:55:49 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2477787

Nvidia shares fell more than two per cent as Wall Street opened on Friday, extending a bruising week for the chip giant after Jensen Huang’s resignation and pushing its market value below $4 trillion. The AI heavyweight slipped 2.5 per cent to around $162 in early trading, having initially risen in pre-market dealings, as investors [...]]]>

Nvidia shares fell more than two per cent as Wall Street opened on Friday, extending a bruising week for the chip giant after Jensen Huang’s resignation and pushing its market value below $4 trillion.

The AI heavyweight slipped 2.5 per cent to around $162 in early trading, having initially risen in pre-market dealings, as investors continued to assess the fallout from the departure of its founder and chief executive after 33 years. He stepped down following reports of multiple extramarital affairs, including a relationship with a woman suspected by US intelligence officials of spying for China.

The decline followed Thursday’s volatile session, when Nvidia shares plunged more than 13 per cent at the opening bell before recovering to close just over four per cent lower.

The scandal has raised questions over Nvidia’s leadership and corporate governance, with chief financial officer Colette Kress taking over as interim chief executive while the board searches for a permanent successor.

Tech stocks retreat as Wall Street opens mixed

The wider US market opened mixed on Friday, with the S&P 500 edging up 0.15 per cent to 7,603.78 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average gaining 0.27 per cent to 52,438.13.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite slipped 0.07 per cent to 25,347.59 as selling pressure continued across semiconductor stocks.

Nvidia’s rivals also lost ground, with AMD, Broadcom and Intel falling around two per cent, reversing some of Thursday’s gains as investors reassessed the sector’s outlook.

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, which produces Nvidia’s chips, slipped less than one per cent, while Dutch chip equipment maker ASML was little changed.

Memory chipmakers Micron Technology and SK Hynix also declined, alongside storage manufacturer SanDisk.

The losses followed a difficult session for Wall Street on Thursday, when the S&P 500 fell 0.35 per cent, and the Dow shed 189 points as Nvidia’s leadership crisis weighed on sentiment.

Despite the sell-off, some analysts believe the chipmaker’s falling valuation could present an opportunity for investors. James Demmert, chief investment officer at Main Street Research, said sentiment towards Nvidia had become “extremely negative”, but suggested the shares could find support around $165.

“We think the stock has support at $165 per share, and sentiment is extremely negative,” he said on Friday morning.

Nvidia chief’s defenestration underlines the importance of governance ESG’s overlooked category, Ali Lyon writes in today’s Midday Markets newsletter.

At City AM, we pride ourselves on making the cross-pollinating worlds of business, finance, economics and wealth, fun. Indeed, so averse are our higher-ups to conforming to the industries’ love of complexity, jargon and – dare we say – pretence, that ‘business with personality’ has been the paper’s strapline for the entirety of its 21-year existence.

And so when, today, I suggested devoting this newsletter to the the subject of ‘governance’ I was met with more than a few raised eyebrows.

I’ll concede, 700 words on the processes and structures that a company implements to protect the long-term interests of its stakeholders doesn’t scream ‘business with personality’.

But this week’s defenestration of Jensen Huang – the scandal-hit co-founder of chip giant Nvidia – has thrust the thorny, unsexy issue firmly into the limelight, and thrown up some interesting talking points, to boot.

To many in the public and among some of the company’s shareholders, Huang was not the face of Nvidia; he was Nvidia. And for good reason: the leather jacket-toting, ever-energetic ‘AI rockstar’ had been both chief executive and president of the semiconductor colossus for more than 30 years.

He oversaw its evolution from niche computer-gaming chipmaker to the undisputed weathermaker of the AI evolution. And now, he’s gone, leaving a vacuum of leadership, not just at the world’s second-largest company, but at the heart of the most financially consequential industrial revolution in history.

This is, to borrow a technical phrase, not good. Nvidia’s shares are down 10 per cent since the start of the week, and 20 per cent in the past month. In one day, they shed more value than the total market capitalisation of HSBC, the FTSE 100’s most valuable company, all because of the poor judgement of a single, highly consequential individual.

UK Corporate Governance Code, I was not familiar with your game

The unseemly episode has laid bare the sheer amount of power and influence wielded by those at the top of the largest companies in history. In Nvidia’s case, Huang reportedly had up to 60 executives reporting directly into him at any one time. And despite the totemic founder’s multi-decade tenure, Nvidia’s toothless – and, until this week, chairless – board appears to have done next to no succession planning.

As Imperial Business School associate professor Dr Porneetha Luthra wrote in the pages of City AM this week: “While charismatic’ leaders can seem intoxicating – admired, respected and sometimes loved – this is a very dangerous hierarchy.”

It’s worth noting that, had the same indiscretions been committed by any of the other founder-led tech giants, things would have been even worse. Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg, SpaceX and Tesla’s Elon Musk and Palantir’s Alex Karp are all, essentially, impossible to fire, thanks to the company’s dual-share structure.

And to a number, those emblematic entrepreneurs also personally own much more of the company than Huang’s 3.6 per cent. Just imagine the chaos had it been Elon Musk – who owns a fifth of Tesla and nearly half of SpaceX – who fraternised with an alleged Chinese spy.

In the good times, this concentrated power is a blessing. It allows for fast, bold decision-making unhindered by pesky shareholder votes and board oversight. When you’re dealing with some of the biggest brains in the world, who know their company and industry back to front – those decisions are more often than not, correct and lucrative. But either in – or in the run-up to – crises, robust governance is worth its weight in gold.

Which is why, today at least, we should be grateful for the UK’s rather old-fashioned approach. Thanks to the UK Corporate Governance Code, there is not a single FTSE 100 chief executive who also serves as chair of their company’s board (on the US’s S&P 500, more than four in 10 do). Under London-listing rules, any public company that allows its most senior executive to serve in both roles must explain its rationale to shareholders every year.

In a recent overhaul, the London Stock Exchange chose to water down some of its rules in what is, so far, a vein attempt to attract founder-led fintech and tech unicorn IPOs. But those changes don’t come close to mirroring the free-wheeling approach adopted by the bourse’s counterparts across the pond. And after this week’s Nvidious episode, that is probably no bad thing.

Often in politics, people look to you to be excessively partisan. As someone who came to politics only after a career in business, that isn’t my style. I welcome the positives from this week’s GDP figures whilst cautioning ministers trying to take a celebratory lap from a decidedly mixed picture.

First, let’s consider what this week’s figures show: 0.7 per cent growth in Q3 of 2026, up from 0.5 per cent in Q2. Compared to last year, that’s GDP 1.9 per cent higher. This is by no means a boom, nor is it far off from expectations, but in the context of global shocks and rising inflation, it is still welcome. The devil is, as ever, in the details which show a deeply uneven picture across the economy.

The ONS data shows that big growth drivers have been tech and business services, including IT and computer equipment. These benefit from the global AI boom and Britain’s services sector is well placed to catch it, especially because our position outside the EU has kept us safe from overzealous AI regulation. The key then, is to let this winner run.

Last week, the Bank of England estimated that AI-related activity accounts for a staggering fifth of all growth since the start of the year. An EU reset that jeopardises that growth by adopting Brussels regulations could be enormously damaging.  

The worrying trends behind the figures

Now for the less good news: behind the headline figures there lies the continuation of some worrying trends.  

The resolutely domestic construction sector shrank by 0.7 per cent in Q3, under a government that promised to get Britain building. In fact, construction sector indices have been in negative territory ever since Labour took office. The Office for Budget Responsibility now expects 190,000 fewer new builds than it forecast as recently as March. It’s a big sector of the economy and one at the sharp end of government policy. The verdict isn’t good.

The macroeconomic picture also shows up an oddity. Unpicking the public and private sector components of GDP, it becomes clear that the former has soared while the latter has flagged. Public sector spending and investment have grown 20 per cent since 2019, while the same components in the private sector have only grown 3.2 per cent. This is not a wholly new problem, but it is getting worse not better. It is no more sustainable than a hungry snake eating its own tail.

Brits are still being squeezed

Finally, in the real world, families are bracing for harder months ahead, with expensive energy bills, inflation remaining high and rising interest rates. The households and businesses that have kept this economy moving are about to be squeezed even further, which is why today is no moment for a victory lap.

The tangible help the economy urgently needs is to cut energy costs by getting Britain drilling again and removing the tangled web of levies and obligations that have held back industry and raised costs for families. Second, lift the ongoing burden on employers from Labour’s ‘back to the 1970s’ (Un)Employment Act alongside adopting the Conservative policy halving the jobs tax for young people. And to help construction, speed up planning and cut gold plated regulations to get Britain building again.

This week’s growth figures remain a testament to the strength and resilience of British businesses. Such growth as there is has come despite, not because of, the government. Just imagine what those businesses could do with a government properly on their side.

Andrew Griffith is shadow chancellor

    Criminal defence barristers like Ian Winter KC should not face public condemnation simply for vigorously fulfilling their professional duty to hold the prosecution to account, even when representing famous clients like Russell Brand, says Luke Gittos

    It has been a tough week for Ian Winter KC, counsel for disgraced comedian Russell Brand. His client was convicted last Thursday of rape and three sexual assaults. On Monday, Brand was sentenced to ten years and six months. Whilst making  a point in mitigation, arguing that Brand’s behaviour did not constitute a continuous course of conduct, the Judge pushed back saying “the fact that he got away with it for so long is hardly mitigation, is it?”. 

    The Judge was not the first person to stick the boot into Winter. He has been condemned for confronting Sunday Times journalist Rosamund Urwin outside Southwark Crown Court, apparently blaming her reporting for denying Brand a fair trial. He has referred himself to the Bar Standards Board. Reports have also emerged of his unsuccessful pre-trial abuse of process application, in which he accused journalists from the Times newspapers and Channel 4 of criminal conduct. His questioning of the complainants has been labelled aggressive and demeaning. Brand himself is reportedly unhappy with his representation and considering a new legal team.

    These criticisms are misplaced. Consider the abuse-of-process application first. Brand faced extraordinary publicity long before a jury was sworn. An argument that this publicity might compromise the fairness of his trial was plainly worth considering. That is exactly what an abuse of process application can address: whether proceedings can fairly continue. Winter went further, alleging that the journalists’ reporting amounted to contempt of court and perverting the course of justice. That is a serious allegation, but it should not obscure the perfectly proper question of whether Brand could receive a fair trial after years of publicity. It was a reasonable argument to make, albeit that Winter made it in strong terms. 

    As for Winter’s trial tactics, let us at least accept that he had a difficult job. The prosecution presented Brand as a serial sexual predator who had escaped accountability for years. Women had independently come forward describing similar conduct. That was a formidable case to meet. Brand denied the offences, maintaining that sexual encounters were consensual or that the alleged incidents had not happened. His defence necessarily involved challenging the complainants’ credibility.

    You can’t call someone a liar politely

    Winter did so forcefully. But it is difficult to call someone a liar politely. Where his instructions required him to allege dishonesty, he had a professional duty to put the substance of that allegation to the witness. A barrister cannot abandon an accused person’s defence because it makes for uncomfortable headlines.

    Of course, that duty has limits. The rules on questioning complainants in sexual cases have changed substantially. Barristers cannot humiliate witnesses for sport. Judges warn juries against rape myths, including assumptions about how a genuine victim must behave. There is no automatic entitlement to ask any question simply because it might help the defence. But robust cross-examination remains essential, especially where the defendant disputes the truth of an allegation.

    Imagine that your son or daughter faced a serious charge based on an accusation they insisted was false. You would want their advocate to test that accusation thoroughly; however unpleasant the process became

    Imagine that your son or daughter faced a serious charge based on an accusation they insisted was false. You would want their advocate to test that accusation thoroughly; however unpleasant the process became. That principle does not disappear when the defendant is famous, unpopular or ultimately convicted.

    Winter has acknowledged that his encounter with Urwin deserves scrutiny. Fair enough. His courtroom arguments can also be criticised on their merits. But treating every uncomfortable question and unsuccessful application as evidence of misconduct betrays a misunderstanding of criminal defence. Winter’s task was to make the prosecution prove its case. The jury convicted Brand after hearing that defence. That is how justice works. We should stop attacking barristers simply for doing their jobs.

    Luke Gittos is a litigation partner at Murray Hughman

    Abolishing inheritance tax would help reduce wealth inequality by serving as a crucial equalising measure and source of start-up funding that disproportionately benefits lower-wealth households and middle-class families, says Max Young

    The Chancellor did not abolish Inheritance Tax at the Budget, nor did he lower it. He should know for next time that such a policy would not only provide “growth in every postcode” but would actually reduce inequality in Britain. How so? 

    A landmark 2021 report by the OECD found that “While lower-wealth households receive smaller inheritances and gifts, these are typically large as a share of net wealth.” It added “even a small inheritance can be substantial relative to pre-inheritance wealth.” 

    In the 12 countries examined by the organisation, the second-poorest fifth of households benefited more from their inheritance than the richest fifth. In Spain, 95.6 per cent of the net wealth of the second fifth derived from bequests. 

    In short, the poorer you are, the more important the money your parents pass down to you is. In many cases it will be the only cash injection you ever receive. 

    Richer heirs tend already to own wealth before their parents die. That means inheritances are actually a crucial equalising measure. The evidence bears this out. 

    An 2016 study by the Institute for Fiscal Studies noted that inheritances in Britain “act to make the distribution of non-pension wealth less unequal.” 

    In Denmark, tax record research found that bequests cut the share of wealth held by the top one per cent by around six percentage points. 

    In an analysis of the whole Swedish population’s tax records, inheritances were found to reduce the Gini coefficient, the formula by which relative wealth inequality is measured, by five to ten per cent. 

    The Swedes abolished their tax on inheritances thanks to the fact it had an outsized effect on middle earning families, who paid an effective rate of 5.4 per cent in 2004, up from 2.9 per cent in 1992. The left-wing Social Democratic government scrapped it with the support of two-thirds of Swedes. 

    In Britain, Inheritance Tax hits the middle class the hardest too – HMRC data shows families with estates worth between £2m and £7.5m are hit with an IHT bill of more than 25 per cent, a share which drops for wealthier estates. 

    The 10 countries that have scrapped inheritance tax

    Ten OECD countries have scrapped inheritance taxes: Mexico (1961), Canada (1972), Australia (1979), Israel (1980), New Zealand (1992), Sweden and Slovakia (2004), Austria (2008), the Czech Republic and Norway (2014). There’s a hint for Healey in there somewhere.

    Bequests are a source of crucial start-up funding. A recent survey by Charles Stanley found that 20 per cent of business owners used an inheritance to start their firm, only one point behind bank funding. Some 15 per cent of owners used inheritance cash to fund a later expansion of their business. 

    A 2018 study which examined US data from 1992 to 2010 found that receiving any inheritance increases your chances of owning and running a business by almost 13 per cent. The size mattered comparatively little, too. Each extra $1m bequeathed added only one per cent to that probability. 

    Who benefits most? Banks like to lend against a house or significant savings. Those who have neither rely especially on what their parents leave behind for them. 

    Instead of winding down the tax the British government is expanding it. Unspent pension pots will join the estate from April 2027, too. The Office for Budget Responsibility predicts that more than 10 per cent of British estates will pay Inheritance Tax in three years, thanks to the allowance threshold having been frozen since 2009. It should be more than £540,000 today. 

    Inheritance tax is one of the levies most hated by the British public, because it punishes aspiration and inhibits the basic human desire to provide for one’s children and leave a legacy. It is also helping to keep the poor in relative poverty. Any progressive campaigner worth their salt should campaign for its abolition.

    Max Young is news editor at Guido Fawkes

    With public finances stretched, few expect October’s Budget to be the last word from Andy Burnham’s government on taxing wealth. The wealthy were spared the higher capital gains tax and annual wealth levies championed by some civil society groups inside and outside of the Labour party. But the Budget halved the lifetime limit on Business Asset Disposal Relief to £500,000 and raised tax on savings and property income.

    Wealth taxes need to be treated with caution. High-net-worth individuals (HNWIs) are often business owners or directors who contribute significantly to the economy. The top one per cent already pay about 27 per cent of all income tax, and the top 10 per cent nearly three-fifths. They anchor luxury spending, high-end property and VAT-heavy services like private schooling, and they disproportionately fund private healthcare. 

    The abolition of the 200-year-old “non-domicile” status is widely reported to have prompted departures and capital flight. The departures and capital flight caused by the abolition of non-dom status are not just anecdotal. Henley & Partners estimated a net outflow of 16,500 millionaires from the UK in 2025, which it said would be the largest recorded. European visa schemes, Dubai’s 0 per cent personal tax, Swiss stability and US states like Florida and Texas are all said to have drawn wealth away.

    What about the wealthy who stay?

    Those who stay need confidence in the economy and sufficient liquidity to run their businesses and investments as costs rise. Since April 2025, businesses have absorbed higher employer National Insurance, followed this April by a higher minimum wage, a business rates revaluation and a tougher inheritance tax regime. Borrowing is also dearer: the Bank of England raised rates by 0.25 percentage points to four per cent on 5 November, its first increase since 2023, as higher energy costs pushed inflation well above its two per cent target.

    Higher taxes and rising costs make liquidity planning critical. Traditional lenders are unlikely to fill the gap alone: our clients tell us that high-street banks and other traditional lenders have been tightening underwriting, demanding higher debt service coverage ratios and capping loan sizes.

    Liquidity planning

    One option is share-backed lending, sometimes called Lombard lending: borrowing against a holding of listed shares instead of selling it. For a founder facing a tax bill or a funding gap, that can avoid a forced sale and the capital gains tax that comes with it. 

    UK HNWIs may be feeling the pressure as their wealth comes under scrutiny, but they remain vital contributors through the tax they pay, the businesses they run and the sectors they sustain. Business investment is still recovering slowly, and the UK can ill afford to drive away the people responsible for growth.

    Helping HNWIs manage liquidity serves the spenders and the businesses that power the British economy.

    James Mungovan is CEO of Europe for Equities First

    Just over a week ago ministers announced £700m to unlock up to ten major industrial and commercial sites. Welcome news.     A lot has been said, written and done to ensure the 2031 Rugby World Cup is a huge hit in host nation the United States. World Rugby is hoping that staging mega international matches, Nations Championship finals and even domestic fixtures Stateside in the run-up can ensure that there is sufficient appetite for the quadrennial tournament four years on from what is bound to be a money-making success in Australia next autumn.

    But the entire tournament is now at risk of being overshadowed or, worse, forgotten. Because rugby league is looking to steal union’s thunder by hosting part of the 2030 Rugby League World Cup in the United States.

    Early announcements suggest that league could stage Magic Weekend-style match weeks – where six games take place in the same venue over two days – across the United States mainland and, interestingly, a number of Pacific Islands and Hawaii.

    Not only does this tread on longstanding union land – Fiji, Samoa and Tonga have been playing 15s for decades although the latter two are increasingly being seen as league countries – but it also precedes union’s World Cup arrival in the United States.

    League vs union

    And while rugby union has staged international matches and hosted Prem Rugby fixtures in the US, league is much more present Stateside these days with an NRL-Super League double header each season in Las Vegas.

    International rugby league also appears to be more palatable for US sports fans. The rules are much more simple than both rugby union and the NFL, it is as physical as the others and it largely relies on simply counting to six. Even the newest of sports fans can do that.

    Union, on the other hand, is a complex and nuanced being with every decision often one that has an argument for it to have been given the other way. 

    Union risks being left behind by rugby league and there is little it can do about it: making a noise may be offputting but failing to out-perform its rival World Cup having had the advantage of seeing what league offers could kill off the sport for an entire continent.

    What rugby union has which league can only dream of, however, is a strong domestic game. Across Europe, the southern hemisphere and Japan there are competitive leagues with a proper presence elsewhere – including in the United States’ Major League Rugby competition. 

    United States showdown

    England’s Super League hasn’t finalised a broadcast deal for next season yet – it is expected to be shared by Dazn and Sky Sports – and hasn’t yet formalised its structure or number of teams amid investment interest from the Australian NRL.

    But even now the international game in rugby union is starting to suffocate that of rugby league. Did anyone know there was a Rugby League World Cup final this weekend, and has anybody watched much of the Premier Sports coverage? 

    Rugby union in Britain is currently enjoying its Saturdays being completely booked out by ITV for the Nations Championship – live rugby on terrestrial television from 12 noon through to 10pm every weekend this month. League could only dream of that.

    Rugby union will not yet worry about its sibling; international rugby league is too small to be a commercial or broadcast threat while the domestic game isn’t wholesale enough to dent World Rugby coffers.

    But bosses must be watchful of plans to take league World Cup matches to both union heartlands and areas the 15s game will be targeting within the next five years. Because to allow rugby league a head start is for rugby union to shoot itself in the foot. And it’s got far too much history of that for it to be unthinkable.

Most people protect their digital lives with a handful of passwords they've memorized—a security practice so common it's become catastrophic.]]>

For about five months, a browser extension sat quietly on the home computers of 154 people and watched them log in.

The researchers never saw a password. Everything was hashed on the machine before it went anywhere, leaving them with the shape of each one: its length, its mix of characters, the site it was typed into, and whether the same string had appeared before.

Very often, it had.

What 154 people actually typed

Sarah Pearman and her co-authors at Carnegie Mellon University presented the results at a 2017 computer security conference, having followed each participant for an average of 147 days. Those people logged in across 26 web domains apiece and covered the lot with fewer than 10 distinct passwords.

Roughly 60 per cent of those distinct passwords were recycled, either typed identically on another site or built around a chunk of four or more characters lifted from one the same person used elsewhere.

Banking got no special treatment. Around 85 per cent of the passwords on financial sites appeared elsewhere too, and nearly all of that crossover ran into unrelated categories, so the login for a savings account was also the login for a shoe shop.

What partial reuse looks like up close

Mostly it looks like adding a character.

Among passwords that shared a substring with another, the most common gap between the two was a single character. Digits were the strongest predictor in the Carnegie Mellon model, multiplying the odds of reuse by more than twelve. The authors’ own explanation is that a password with a number in it satisfies more websites’ fussy signup rules, so it travels further.

The tidy minority had barely any accounts

Ten participants mostly built something new for each site, which sounds like a win for good habits until you look at what they were doing online. With one exception, every one of them entered passwords on eight domains or fewer, and they were active on their computers on only 17 per cent of the days they spent enrolled.

The heavy users went the other way. Ninety-four participants, the largest cluster by far, both copied passwords outright and modified them, and they averaged 32 online accounts each. Discipline held up fine at eight accounts and collapsed at thirty.

The password manager result, with a handbrake

Only 19 of the 154 participants had a password manager installed, and the study found no measurable effect on either reuse or strength.

That result deserves caution. One paper is one paper, the subgroup is tiny, and the software could not tell whether people were generating random strings or merely parking passwords they had invented themselves. Rick Wash and colleagues at Michigan State University, who watched 134 participants over six weeks, found each password being reused on 1.7 to 3.4 websites. Their study did not measure partial reuse at all, so the higher figure out of Pittsburgh partly reflects counting a habit nobody had counted before.

Why a recycled password is worth money

Somewhere there is a text file with an old forum password in it, sitting in a folder alongside a few hundred million others. Troy Hunt, the Australian security researcher behind the breach notification service Have I Been Pwned, has documented the trade in combo lists, which are exactly that: vast dumps of email and password pairs scraped out of past breaches. Cheap automated tools fire them at unrelated websites until one opens. Defending against it is awkward, because a successful run looks identical to a customer logging in correctly.

One shared string, and the breach at a defunct hobby forum becomes a problem at an email provider.

The rules that encouraged this have been withdrawn

In 2025, the US National Institute of Standards and Technology finalised revision 4 of its digital identity guidelines, and the password section reads like a quiet apology. Websites must stop demanding mixtures of character types, and they must stop forcing periodic changes unless there is evidence of compromise. Password managers and autofill have to be allowed, and every new password gets checked against blocklists of strings already known to have leaked.

Each of those requirements targets the behaviour the extension recorded: a handful of memorable strings, nudged sideways by a digit, stretched across an entire online life.

The standard now assumes a machine is doing the remembering. Anyone who ever stuck a “1” on the end to get past a signup form was just covering the shift until it arrived.

A Dutch court sided with a worker who refused constant video surveillance, forcing his employer to pay damages—a warning shot across the evolving battle over remote work monitoring.]]>

A camera that stayed switched off cost a Florida software company about 75,000 euros.

It belonged to a telemarketer working from the small Dutch town of Diessen, employed since January 2019 by Chetu, an American software firm that at the time ran a Dutch office in Rijswijk. On 23 August 2022 he was told to join something called the Corrective Action Program, which meant staying logged in for his whole shift, sharing his screen and leaving his laptop camera on. He shared the screen. The camera stayed dark.

His objection was brief and entirely unlegalistic. Court filings quoted by The Register record him saying he was not comfortable being monitored for nine hours a day, calling it “an invasion of my privacy” and noting that his laptop activity was already visible to management.

Two more instructions followed, each firmer than the last. On 26 August he was dismissed on the spot, the stated reasons being refusal to work and insubordination.

Three days from the first instruction to the sack.

What the company argued

Chetu’s case, set out in the published judgment of the Court of Zeeland-West-Brabant, was that watching a remote worker through a webcam is no different from a manager walking past a desk. Performance software already sat on the man’s laptop, and that was not considered enough. Chetu wanted to see him working.

Nobody from the company turned up to make the argument in person, as TechCrunch noted, so it went undefended.

What the judge decided

Ruling on 28 September 2022, the subdistrict judge in Tilburg found that ordering an employee to keep a camera running for a full shift conflicted with his right to respect for private life, and that nothing had been offered to justify it. An unreasonable instruction cannot be unreasonably refused, so there had been no refusal to work and no grounds for summary dismissal.

Data protection law dropped out early. On the understanding that no footage would be recorded, stored or used for anything, the judge treated the monitoring as falling outside data processing altogether, and tested it directly against Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, alongside Strasbourg case law holding that filming staff at work, covert or not, is a serious intrusion into private life. Had the images been kept, the analysis would have looked quite different.

One much-quoted line deserves care. Coverage including a report in Fortune presented the claim that all-day camera tracking is disproportionate and not allowed in the Netherlands as a finding of the court. In the Dutch record it sits among the employee’s own submissions. What the judge actually held was narrower, and sufficient: this instruction, to this man, in his own home, breached Article 8 with no justification advanced.

Why the sum was so large

Almost none of the money was a penalty for the privacy breach. The largest slice, 50,000 euros, was a billijke vergoeding, an equitable award Dutch judges reserve for employers whose conduct in ending a job has been seriously culpable, with a wrongful summary dismissal among the standard triggers, as the Amsterdam employment firm Workx Advocaten explains. Privacy is why the sacking failed. The sacking is what got billed.

A Dutch judge has now looked at that question once, and the employer left lighter.

Estonia’s population stood at 1,360,745 at the start of 2026, according to Statistics Estonia. That is smaller than many single cities. Out of it has come ten companies that reached a billion-dollar valuation at some point in their history, among them Skype, Wise, Bolt, Pipedrive, Playtech and Veriff, according to Invest in Estonia’s own tally.

Using CB Insights’ underlying company data alongside that population figure, a figure Invest in Estonia and outlets including Fintech Baltic put at roughly 7.1 unicorns per million residents, based on Invest in Estonia’s cumulative count of companies that have ever reached $1B — not a live ranking CB Insights itself publishes, second only to Liechtenstein and more than three times the United States’ rate of about 2.2 per million.

The tiger leap that came before the unicorns

This density didn’t happen by accident, and it didn’t start with a startup. In 1996, five years after regaining independence from the Soviet Union, Estonia launched a state programme called Tiigrihüpe, or Tiger Leap, championed by future president Toomas Hendrik Ilves and education minister Jaak Aaviksoo. Its goal was blunt: wire the country’s schools for computers and the internet as a deliberate act of catching up. It worked faster than almost anyone expected.

The rollout was rapid but not instantaneous. Education Estonia says all schools had computers by 2000 and all were connected to the internet by 2001. It wasn’t only talent that recirculated. Toivo Annus, one of Skype’s founding engineers who led its engineering team until the eBay sale, went on to co-found Ambient Sound Investments with three other early Skype engineers in 2003, a private investment firm that has since backed more than 50 early-stage ventures, according to documented accounts of his career. The ecosystem underneath those ten companies is larger and more active than the unicorn count alone suggests. A per-capita unicorn count says nothing about how many of those companies are still worth a billion dollars today, still headquartered in Estonia, or profitable. Playtech moved its primary listing to London years ago. Skype no longer trades as an independent business at all. For a country with fewer people than a mid-sized American county, that is the more durable claim.

An hour disappears into the phone and the honest inventory afterwards runs to three items: a man cutting marble, somebody’s strong opinion about interest rates, a dog on a skateboard.

None of it is retained in any way worth having. The hour still lands like work.

That mismatch, between the feeling of effort and the absence of anything learned, has a reasonable research explanation behind it, and willpower barely features in it.

A feed is a run of cold starts

Reading a book is one long continuous job. The brain loads a setting, a cast, an argument, and then keeps using that same setup for as long as the reading lasts.

A feed offers nothing of the kind.

Each post arrives with its own subject, tone, format and rules, which means the machinery of attention has to reconfigure itself before any of the content can be processed.

A feed adds another recurring job: a verdict. Each item has to be sized up for whether it is true, whether it is funny, whether it is aimed at anyone in particular. That call gets made before the thing can be dismissed, and then made again at the next one, and the one after that.

Psychologists have taken that reconfiguration apart. In a paper published in the Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance, Joshua Rubinstein, David Meyer and Jeffrey Evans described two stages: goal shifting, meaning the decision to do this now instead of that, and rule activation, meaning the swap of mental instructions from the old job to the new one. Both stages take time. A single switch might cost only a few tenths of a second. That sounds trivial until you count the switches inside an hour of scrolling.

Their experiments used arithmetic and shape-sorting rather than phones, so applying the finding to a feed is an inference, not a measurement.
